course.title: Game Design and Game Programming Patterns
course.description: What makes a game work as play, and what makes its code survive growth. Five lessons on loops, feedback, difficulty, balance and testing, then seven on the architecture patterns behind most games, in any engine.
course.audience: A capable adult who plays games and has written some code, and wants to design systems and structure programs the way game developers do. They can read short Python or pseudocode and have met functions, objects and arrays. No engine, editor or art skills are assumed.

paragraphs: A jump in a platform game is two things at once. For the player it is an experience, which feels crisp or heavy according to how many frames pass between the press of the button and the first movement of the character. For the program it is a state that the character enters, which some states can reach and others cannot, and which has to keep working as the game grows to hundreds of kinds of object. Game design is the study of how rules produce the first, and game programming patterns are the standard arrangements of code that keep the second manageable.

Qualities that players describe only loosely often have numbers behind them. A control that feels heavy can be traced to a delay counted in frames, and a fight that drags to the ratio of the enemy's health to the damage dealt each second. Once a quality has a number, two versions of a game can be compared on paper, and a prototype or a playtest can then show whether the number matches what players feel.

The code has recurring problems of its own, and a pattern is a standard arrangement of code for one of them, together with what the arrangement costs. A character whose behaviour is held in one state variable cannot be in a combination of states that makes no sense, and a grid that files entities by position avoids most of the collision tests that comparing every pair would need when the entities are spread out. None of this depends on an engine, since Godot, Unity and Unreal are current examples of where the ideas are used and every example can be followed in any language by reading short pseudocode or Python.
outcomes: You'll be able to describe a game as mechanics, dynamics and aesthetics, and find its core loop.
You'll be able to explain why a control feels good or bad using response, feedback and timing, and measure it in frames.
You'll be able to tune a number (damage, cost, growth, drop rate) using expected value and growth curves, and predict time-to-kill.
You'll be able to write a fixed-timestep game loop and say what the accumulator does.
You'll be able to choose between a state machine, command, component, event queue, object pool and spatial grid for a stated problem and trace each by hand.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on How Computers Solve Problems, Python for Data Analysis.

modules.title: Designing play
modules.description: Loops, feedback, difficulty, balance and testing, with the numbers that tune them.

modules.title: The shape of a game's code
modules.description: The game loop, state machines, commands and components.

modules.title: Decoupling and speed

concepts.title: MDA
concepts.summary: Mechanics are the rules and data, dynamics are the behaviour that emerges when play runs, aesthetics are the emotional responses of the player.

concepts.title: Core loop
concepts.summary: The short repeated cycle of action, feedback and reward that the player performs most often.

concepts.title: Outer loops
concepts.summary: Longer cycles, such as upgrades or unlocks, that give the core loop a reason to repeat.

concepts.title: Game feel
concepts.summary: The tactile quality of controlling something in real time, set by input, response and context (Swink).

concepts.title: Latency in frames
concepts.summary: Delay from input to visible response, counted in frames: frames = delay in ms ÷ frame time in ms.

concepts.title: Feedback layers
concepts.summary: Visual, audio and haptic cues that confirm an action and its result.

concepts.title: Flow
concepts.summary: A state of absorption that arises when challenge matches skill and goals and feedback are clear (Csikszentmihalyi).

concepts.title: Difficulty curve
concepts.summary: How challenge rises across a game, usually in waves of tension and relief.

concepts.title: Dynamic difficulty adjustment
concepts.summary: Changing challenge in response to measured player performance.

concepts.title: Expected value
concepts.summary: The probability-weighted average outcome of a random effect.

concepts.title: Time to kill
concepts.summary: Target health divided by damage per second.

concepts.title: Growth curve
concepts.summary: A formula, often exponential, for how cost or power rises with level.

concepts.title: Sources and sinks
concepts.summary: Where a resource enters the game and where it leaves; balance means they roughly offset.

concepts.title: Prototype
concepts.summary: A cheap, quick version built to answer one design question.

concepts.title: Playtest
concepts.summary: Observing players who do not know the game, to see where they misunderstand or stall.

concepts.title: Telemetry
concepts.summary: Logged in-game events that show where players fail or quit.

concepts.title: Game loop
concepts.summary: A loop that processes input, updates the world and renders, decoupled from the speed of the machine.

concepts.title: Fixed timestep
concepts.summary: Updates always advance the simulation by the same amount, so results do not depend on frame rate.

concepts.title: Accumulator (lag)
concepts.summary: Unspent real time carried between frames; each update spends one step from it.

concepts.title: Finite state machine
concepts.summary: An object that is in exactly one of a fixed set of states, with transitions between them triggered by events.

concepts.title: State pattern
concepts.summary: Each state is its own object or function that handles input and update for that state.

concepts.title: Hierarchical states
concepts.summary: Substates share behaviour from a parent state, which avoids duplicating transitions.

concepts.title: Command pattern
concepts.summary: A request wrapped as an object, so it can be stored, queued, replayed or undone.

concepts.title: Input binding
concepts.summary: A table mapping inputs to commands, so keys can be rebound without editing game logic.

concepts.title: Undo stack
concepts.summary: A list of executed commands; undo pops and reverses the last one, and a new command clears the redo branch.

concepts.title: Component pattern
concepts.summary: An entity is built from independent components, each handling one concern such as physics or rendering.

concepts.title: Entity component system
concepts.summary: Entities are ids, components are plain data stored by type, and systems loop over entities that have the needed components.

concepts.title: Data locality
concepts.summary: Data stored contiguously is fetched in cache lines (commonly 64 bytes) and processed faster than scattered data.

concepts.title: Observer
concepts.summary: A subject notifies registered listeners when something happens, without knowing what they do.

concepts.title: Event queue
concepts.summary: Events are stored and handled later, decoupling sender from receiver in time as well as in code.

concepts.title: Ring buffer
concepts.summary: A fixed array where the write index wraps to zero after reaching the end.

concepts.title: Object pool
concepts.summary: A fixed set of pre-allocated objects reused instead of created and freed during play.

concepts.title: Flyweight
concepts.summary: Shared immutable data kept once and referenced by many instances.

concepts.title: Fragmentation
concepts.summary: Free memory broken into small gaps that cannot hold a new large object.

concepts.title: Pairwise checks
concepts.summary: Checking every entity against every other takes n(n − 1)/2 tests.

concepts.title: Uniform grid
concepts.summary: The world is divided into equal cells and each entity is stored in the cell holding its position.

concepts.title: Quadtrees and BSP
concepts.summary: Hierarchical partitions that subdivide dense regions further.

lessons.title: Mechanics, dynamics and the core loop

lead.text: Tetris has a board ten squares wide, pieces made of four squares each, controls that move and turn the falling piece, a rule that a completed row disappears, and a rule that the game ends when the pile reaches the top. These rules, together with the data they work on, such as the width of the board and the shape of each piece, are called the game's **mechanics**.

"A jump costs 10 stamina" is a mechanic, because it is a rule with a number in it that a program can check on every jump. The art, the story and the feeling of playing are not mechanics, and neither is fun.

reveal.text: That count is easy to write down, but fitting the pieces together without a gap is another matter, and the next screen is about what players do because of it.

lead.text: Forty squares make exactly ten pieces, but only if every piece fits against its neighbours with no gap, and the shapes seldom allow that. A row of ten is not a multiple of four, so pieces have to straddle rows, and a single hole can stay buried because the rule clears only rows that are *complete*. Players find this out quickly and respond with habits: they keep the surface of the stack flat, they leave one column open for a long piece, and they hurry when the stack nears the top. Behaviour of this kind, which emerges when the rules are played, is called the game's **dynamics**.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows two stacks that obey every rule. In the flat one every empty square can still be reached from above, whereas the other has a hole under a filled square, which no clear can reach until the rows above it have gone. The rules treat the two stacks alike, and **the difference between them lives only in how people play**.

diagram.alt: Two stacks on a ten-square-wide board. The first has no holes. The second has a marked empty square under a filled one, which cannot be reached.
diagram.caption: The rules treat the two stacks alike. Players do not, and that difference in behaviour is a dynamic.

reveal.text: The layer is the one that grows out of the rules rather than being written into them, and the same test sorts the other statements in this lesson.

lead.text: The third layer is what the player feels. Tetris produces challenge, because the pile rises faster than a hesitant player can clear it, and a kind of sensation in the rhythm of dropping, turning and clearing. These feelings are the game's **aesthetics**, a word that here means emotional response and not visual style. The framework comes from a paper that Robin Hunicke, Marc LeBlanc and Robert Zubek presented in 2004, and it lists eight kinds, among them sensation, fantasy, narrative, challenge, fellowship, discovery, expression and submission.

A designer can only write mechanics, so the designer works from the mechanics through the dynamics they are expected to give rise to, towards the aesthetics hoped for, while a player begins with a feeling and sees the rules underneath only after long play.

afterFigure.text: This is why fun cannot be a mechanic: a rule can only make a behaviour more or less likely, and the behaviour in turn makes a feeling more or less likely. **Every design decision is therefore a prediction** that has to be tested by watching people play.

reveal.text: Only one of the four is a feeling. The others are written by the designer or arise from play, which is why a designer cannot write the feeling directly.

lead.text: Take a platformer in which the player jumps, lands on a platform, collects a coin and sees the score rise, and then jumps again. The short cycle the player repeats most often, made of an action, the feedback that follows it and a reward, is the game's **core loop**.

The loop has to come back to its start *with something changed*: after the coin the score is higher and the player stands on a new platform. A list of features such as jumping, coins, a score display and a pause menu is not a loop, because it does not say what leads to what or where the player ends up.

afterFigure.text: **Order and return** are what turn the list into a loop.

steps.headline: Find the core loop of a game in which the player swaps two neighbouring tiles to line up three of the same colour.

workedSteps.text: Ask first what the player does most often. Here it is swapping two tiles, so the action is the swap.
The matched tiles vanish with a sound and a flash, and the player sees at once what the swap did. This part of the loop shows the result of the action.
Points are added and new tiles fall into the gaps, which is the reward, and it also leaves the board in a different arrangement.

The player now looks at the new board and chooses another swap, so the cycle has returned to its first step with the state changed. Opening the settings menu is not part of it, because the player does not pass through it on every cycle.

steps.headline: Follow the platformer loop for several passes and watch the state it leaves behind each time.

workedSteps.text: The score starts at 0 and the player jumps.
The jump lands on a platform with a coin, the coin is collected, and the score rises by 10. The loop is back at the jump with a score of 10.
Each further pass adds the same 10 points. Work out the score after 6 passes in all.

lead.text: The core loop lasts seconds, and a player repeats it hundreds of times in one sitting, so games build longer cycles around it. Collected coins may buy an upgrade, upgrades open a harder level, and finishing levels unlocks a new ability, and each of these is a loop in its own right whose reward changes what the core loop is like the next time. They are called **outer loops**, and are sometimes called meta loops.

afterFigure.text: If one pass of the core loop takes about 5 seconds, a level of 60 seconds holds 12 passes, and an unlock after every 6 levels arrives every 360 seconds, or 6 minutes.

diagram.alt: Nested rounded rectangles. The innermost is the core loop of about five seconds. Around it is one level of 60 seconds. The outermost is an unlock every six levels.
diagram.caption: Each ring is a longer cycle that wraps the one inside it. Use the buttons to add the rings.

reveal.text: The unlock cycle is far longer than the core loop, so it can give the core loop a reason to repeat without taking its place as the thing the player does most often.

lessons.orientation: Describe a game as mechanics, dynamics and aesthetics, and find the loop at its centre.
lessons.reviewLabel: Mechanics, dynamics and the core loop
lessons.nextAction: Judge a control by its response delay in frames and by the layers of feedback it gives.

blocks.text: In Tetris, a row of ten squares that has been filled completely disappears, and everything above it drops down by one row. That is a single sentence of rules, yet it is enough to produce a game in which players learn to keep their stack flat, panic as it climbs, and feel relief when a long piece arrives at the right moment. Nobody wrote "keep the stack flat" or "feel relief" into the program, because those arise from the rule once a person starts to play.

Designers have words for the distance between what is written and what is felt. In a framework presented in 2004, the **mechanics** are the rules that were written, the **dynamics** are the behaviour that appears once people play by them, and the **aesthetics** are the feelings that behaviour produces. A designer can write only the mechanics, so everything the player eventually feels has to be reached by choosing rules and predicting what people will do with them.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to sort a statement about a game into mechanic, dynamic or aesthetic, and to find the core loop and the outer loops around it.
intro.whyItMatters: A designer who cannot tell a rule from the behaviour it causes will fix the wrong thing when a game plays badly.

recap.keyIdea: A game's mechanics are its rules, its dynamics are the behaviour those rules produce in play, its aesthetics are the feelings that result, and the core loop is the short cycle of action, feedback and reward that returns the player to the same action with the state changed.

blocks.text: The rules are the only layer a designer writes directly, so every other layer has to be reached by way of them and then checked by watching play. The core loop is the part of play repeated most often, and the longer outer loops, such as unlocks, are what give a repeated loop its purpose.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks closely at feedback, the second step of the core loop, and asks how long a control takes to answer and why that delay can be measured in frames.

lessons.title: Feedback and game feel

lead.text: Press the jump button in two versions of the same game. In one the character leaves the ground on the very next frame, and in the other six frames later, and the first still feels like part of the player's hand while the second feels like pushing on something heavy. That quality of controlling something in real time is called **game feel**, and Steve Swink's book *Game Feel* (2008) divides it into three parts: the **input** the player gives, the **response** the game makes, and the context in which the two happen.
Response has a beginning, which is how soon after the input anything visible changes, and a shape, which is how the motion unfolds, and the beginning is counted in frames.

reveal.text: That length is the unit in which a response is measured, and the next screen uses it to convert between milliseconds and frames.

lead.text: The time from pressing a button to seeing the result is called **latency**. Designers count it in frames because the game can only change what is on screen once per frame, so a response cannot arrive between two of them. The conversion is a division: a frame lasts 1000 ÷ the frame rate in milliseconds, and the number of frames in a delay is the delay in milliseconds divided by that frame time.

afterFigure.text: At 60 frames per second a frame lasts 16.67 ms, so a delay of 100 ms is 100 ÷ 16.67 = 6 frames, the delay of the second jump in the opening figure. The conversion also runs the other way: **frames multiplied by the frame time give milliseconds**. The figure shows why the frame rate matters, since the same 100 ms holds only 3 frames at 30 frames per second and 12 at 120.

diagram.alt: Horizontal bars. In the first view each bar is the length of one frame in milliseconds: 33.3 at 30 frames per second, 16.7 at 60 and 8.3 at 120. In the second, a 100 millisecond bar is cut into 3, 6 and 12 frames.

steps.headline: A control starts responding 4 frames after the press, on a game running at 60 frames per second. How long is that in milliseconds?

workedSteps.text: First find how long one frame lasts at this frame rate.
The delay is made of four of these frames, so go from frames to milliseconds by one operation.
Four frames last 66.7 ms to one decimal place, a delay long enough that careful players can notice it.

steps.headline: A hit pauses the game for 2 frames at 60 frames per second before the enemy flinches. Find the length of the pause.

workedSteps.text: A frame lasts 1000 ÷ 60 ms at this frame rate.
The pause is made of two frames, so work out how many milliseconds it lasts, to one decimal place.

lead.text: A response is built from layers of **feedback**: a visual cue such as a flash or a pose, an audio cue such as a clang, and where the hardware allows, a haptic cue such as a controller vibrating. **Anticipation** is the wind-up before the blow, which tells the player something is about to happen. The **impact** is the moment of contact, often marked by *hit-stop*, a pause of a couple of frames. The **after-effect** is what follows, such as a shake of the screen and a sound that fades.

afterFigure.text: More layers are not automatically better, because a layer that hides the state of the game works against the others.

diagram.alt: Eight numbered frames of a sword swing. Without layers only frame 3 is marked as the hit. With layers, frames 0 to 2 are anticipation, frames 3 and 4 are the impact pause, and frames 5 to 7 are shake and sound.
diagram.caption: The same swing, bare and layered. Use the buttons to switch.

reveal.text: The effect is large and arrives on time, so the fault lies in what it hides and not in how quickly it appears.

lead.text: Smooth does not mean slow: a character may take twenty frames to reach full running speed, but a responsive game starts that motion on the very next frame after the press, so the player sees at once that the input was received.

Good feel also forgives. When a player runs off a ledge and presses jump a moment later, many games keep accepting a jump for a few frames after the edge, a grace window called **coyote time**, after the cartoon animal that hangs in the air after running off a cliff. A window of 6 frames is 100 ms at 60 frames per second.

afterFigure.text: A press at frame 4 falls inside the window and the jump happens, whereas a press at frame 8 is too late, and the player experiences the first as good control without learning that the rule was bent in their favour.

Because a frame lasts longer at the lower rate, a delay fixed in frames is a delay that grows in real time, so a response target is better set in milliseconds.

lessons.orientation: Judge a control by its response delay in frames and by the layers of feedback it gives.
lessons.nextAction: Explain how challenge and skill interact and compare fixed, selectable and adaptive difficulty.

blocks.text: A game running at 60 frames per second redraws the screen sixty times in each second, so it can answer a button press only on one of those redraws and never between them. The delay before the character visibly responds therefore comes in whole frames, and careful players can feel the difference between a jump that leaves the ground on the next frame and one that leaves six frames later. They seldom blame the timing, and describe the character instead, as heavy, floaty or loose.
Designers call this quality **game feel**, and they measure the start of a response in frames, which can be converted to milliseconds when two frame rates have to be compared.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to convert a delay between milliseconds and frames, and to audit a control for its layers of feedback and for effects that hide what the player needs to see.
intro.whyItMatters: Players blame a character for a slow jump, so a delay counted in frames is the first number to check when controls feel wrong.

recap.keyIdea: A control feels responsive when its response begins on the next frame, which is a delay counted as milliseconds ÷ frame time, and when its feedback is layered and legible.

blocks.text: Latency is a number you can measure: a frame lasts 1000 ÷ the frame rate in milliseconds, so the same count of frames is a longer wait at a lower frame rate. The feel around that number comes from layers of feedback, anticipation, impact and after-effect, and from forgiveness such as coyote time, all of which have to leave the player able to see what changed.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns from how a single action feels to how a whole game keeps a player between boredom and frustration.

lessons.title: Challenge, flow and difficulty

lead.text: Place a player on a plane with their skill on one axis and the challenge of what they face on the other. When the challenge is far above the skill, the player feels **anxiety**, and when it is far below, the player feels **boredom**. Between the two lies a diagonal band, and a player inside it, with clear goals and feedback that says how things are going, can become completely absorbed. The psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi named that state **flow**, developing the idea from studies in the 1970s and describing it in his 1990 book *Flow*.

The band is not a fact of nature with exact edges, so a model needs a rule. In this lesson the channel is the set of challenges within 1 point of the player's skill, on a scale from 0 to 10. Real games cannot be measured so neatly, but the picture holds: the same level is anxious for one player, bored for another, and absorbing for a third.

diagram.alt: A plane with skill on the horizontal axis and challenge on the vertical axis. A green diagonal band is the flow channel, with anxiety above it and boredom below. One player is marked as a dot.

reveal.text: The player did nothing wrong, and neither did the level. The gap opened because one number moved and the other stayed still.

lead.text: A fixed challenge drifts into boredom as the player improves, so challenge must rise, and the obvious design is a ramp that climbs steadily from the first level to the last. A steadier ramp is not the better one, though, because a player who climbs without a break gets tired.

afterFigure.text: A familiar alternative is a wave with four beats: a first level introduces one jump, the *teach* beat, a second chains three of them, the *test*, a third adds a moving platform, the *twist*, and a fourth is a quiet room that gives *relief*. The next wave starts higher than the last one did, so the line falls at the end of every wave and **still rises overall**.

steps.headline: A player of skill 8 meets a level of challenge 3. Place the player on the plane and say what they feel.

workedSteps.text: First write down the two numbers, with skill on the horizontal axis and challenge on the vertical axis.
The channel at skill 8 covers challenges from 7 to 9, so compare the level with those edges.
The challenge of 3 is below the lower edge, 4 points short of it, so the player is under the channel. Name the state that goes with that region.

lead.text: With **fixed** difficulty every player meets the same curve, which is simple to design and test but suits only the players it was tuned for. With **selectable** difficulty the player picks a curve at the start, such as easy, normal or hard, though not everyone chooses well. With **dynamic difficulty adjustment** (DDA) the game measures how the player is doing, for example deaths per level, and moves the challenge in response.

afterFigure.text: The adaptive curve moves above and below the planned dashed one, because the game is steering the player back towards the channel.

diagram.alt: Three graphs of challenge over time. Fixed shows one rising line. Selectable shows three lines labelled easy, normal and hard, with normal chosen. Adaptive shows a planned dashed line and a green line that moves above and below it.
diagram.caption: Three ways of setting how hard a game is. Use the buttons to compare them.

reveal.text: The other two are set before play begins, by the designer or by the player, and then stay put.

lead.text: In some racing games the cars that trail the leader are given extra speed so that the race stays close, an adjustment called **rubber-banding**, and players can feel it. A driver who has run a clean race and is overtaken by a car that had been far behind will conclude that the result was not earned.

A player who loses should be able to say why: the jump was mistimed, the enemy was not seen, the health ran out. If the cause is hidden, as it is when the game quietly adjusts the odds, even a perfectly judged difficulty feels arbitrary.

reveal.text: The system may well be measuring correctly. The harm comes when the player can see the hand that is steering.
Because each cut applies to the current health and not to the starting health, the second cut is smaller than the first.

lessons.orientation: Place a player on the flow channel and choose between fixed, selectable and adaptive difficulty.
lessons.nextAction: Compute expected damage, time-to-kill and growth curves to tune a game's numbers.

blocks.text: The same level can absorb a player during their first hour of play and bore them in the next, though nothing in the level has changed. The player has changed: after an hour of practice the jumps that once demanded attention are made without thought, so the level asks less of them than it did, and the part of the experience that came from effort has drained away.

A designer who wants to keep a player engaged has to keep the demands of the game in step with the player's growing ability. The psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi called the state in which the two are matched flow, and a simple version of his picture, with the player's skill on one axis and the challenge of the level on the other, shows when a player will be bored, when anxious and when absorbed.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say whether a player is bored, anxious or in flow from their skill and the challenge, and to choose between fixed, selectable and adaptive difficulty.
intro.whyItMatters: A game tuned for one player is too easy or too hard for the next, so difficulty is a design decision, not a default.

recap.keyIdea: Flow arises when challenge matches skill, so challenge has to rise as the player improves, and it is set by a fixed curve, by the player's choice, or by dynamic adjustment that must stay legible and fair.

blocks.text: The flow channel explains why a fixed challenge drifts from absorbing to boring, and the wave-shaped curve answers it by rising overall while still giving the player valleys of relief. The three ways of setting difficulty trade simplicity against fit, and the adaptive one needs particular care so that players do not catch it steering them.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson puts numbers on a game, including expected damage, time to kill and the growth of costs, so that a designer can predict how hard something is before anyone plays it.

lessons.title: Balance by the numbers

reveal.text: The next screen shows how to combine the two outcomes exactly, and why the right weighting is by how often each one happens.

lead.text: A random effect has several possible results, and its **expected value** is what the results average out to over a very long run. To find it, multiply each result by its probability and add the products. For the sword, nine hits in ten do 50 damage and one in ten does 150, so the expected damage is 0.9 × 50 + 0.1 × 150 = 45 + 15 = 60. No single hit does 60, but a thousand hits will average very close to it.

The weighting matters, and a common mistake is to ignore it. A 10 percent chance of triple damage is not the same as a flat doubling of every hit, since a flat doubling would give 100, and it is not the same as the plain average of 50 and 150 either. **Each outcome counts in proportion to its probability**, and outcomes can be stacked in a figure whose widths are those probabilities.

afterFigure.text: The second view adds a chance to miss, which multiplies the outcomes together: a critical hit requires a hit first, so its probability is 0.8 × 0.1 = 0.08. The contributions then come to 0 + 36 + 12 = 48. The base damage, the hit rate, the crit chance and the crit multiplier together describe one weapon.

diagram.alt: A bar split by probability. In the first view, 90 percent of swings do 50 damage and 10 percent do 150, giving an expected 60. In the second, 20 percent miss, 72 percent hit for 50 and 8 percent hit for 150, giving an expected 48.
diagram.caption: Each outcome contributes its probability times its damage, and the contributions are added. Use the buttons to add a miss chance.

reveal.text: A miss chance scales the whole expected value, so the answer here is the 60 from before multiplied by 0.7, the chance of hitting at all.

lead.text: Expected damage per hit says how strong a single swing is, but a player feels how long a fight lasts. That is the **time to kill**: the target's health divided by the **damage per second**, where damage per second is the expected damage per hit multiplied by the number of hits each second. An enemy with 300 health, hit for 60 expected damage twice a second, takes damage at a rate of 120 per second and dies after 300 ÷ 120 = 2.5 seconds.

afterFigure.text: Without the critical hits the expected damage falls to 45 and the rate to 90 per second, so the time to kill rises to about 3.3 seconds, a third as long again, from a change that looks small on paper.

steps.headline: Find the time to kill an enemy with 450 health, using a weapon with 75 expected damage per hit and 1.5 hits per second.

workedSteps.text: Damage per second comes first: multiply the damage per hit by the hits per second.
The enemy's health is shared out at that rate, so decide which quantity the health is divided by.
Dividing 450 by 112.5 gives the time in seconds.

steps.headline: Find the time to kill an enemy with 240 health, using a weapon that does 40 damage per hit and hits 3 times per second.

workedSteps.text: The damage per second is the damage per hit times the hits per second.
Now divide the health by that rate. Work out the time to kill, in seconds.

lead.text: Upgrades need prices, and the price of each level follows a rule called a **growth curve**. The simplest rule adds the same amount every level, which is linear growth. A rule that multiplies by the same ratio every level is exponential growth: the cost of a level is the base cost times the growth ratio raised to the power of the level minus one. With a base of 100 and a ratio of 1.5, level 3 costs 100 × 1.5² = 100 × 2.25 = 225.

afterFigure.text: At level 6, a ratio of 1.2 gives a cost of about 249, a ratio of 1.5 gives about 759, and a ratio of 2 gives 3200. Designers pick the ratio by asking how long they want a player to spend between upgrades.

reveal.text: Each level costs half as much again as the level before it, so the extra cost at each step is itself getting bigger.

lead.text: Coins, gems and experience points enter the game and leave it, and a designer tracks both. A **source** is anywhere a resource enters, such as a reward for a level, and a **sink** is anywhere it leaves, such as a shop price or a repair bill. If the sources exceed the sinks, players pile up currency and prices lose their meaning, a slide that is called **inflation**. If the sinks exceed the sources, players cannot afford anything and stall.
This is why one stat is never balanced alone: a weapon's damage is balanced relative to the enemies' health, the cost of its upgrades, and the income that pays for them.

afterFigure.text: Formulas such as these are good at finding outliers, but they cannot say whether a fight is fun, so the numbers give a first estimate and playtests judge it.

reveal.text: The surplus does not stay still: it grows every hour, so the longer a player plays, the less a price means.
A fixed ratio passes any ceiling sooner than it seems to, which is why designers check a curve at several levels and not only the first few.

lessons.orientation: Compute expected damage, time to kill and growth in a game's costs.
lessons.nextAction: Build a cheap prototype and run a playtest that answers a question.

blocks.text: A sword does 50 damage, and one hit in ten is a critical hit that does triple damage. The sword has to be priced, compared with a bow and matched against an enemy's health before a single player has swung it, and each of those jobs needs one number that says how strong the sword is.

With that number, multiplying by the swings each second gives the rate at which the sword wears an enemy down, which fixes how long a fight lasts, and a rule for how the price of an upgrade rises with level gives the cost of each step. A few short calculations of this kind produce the first draft of a game's numbers, and a playtest then shows where the draft is wrong.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute expected damage, time to kill and the cost at a given level, and to say where a calculation stops being enough.
intro.whyItMatters: Numbers set the first draft of a game's balance, so a designer who can compute them avoids tuning by guesswork.

recap.keyIdea: Expected damage is the probability-weighted average of the outcomes, time to kill is health divided by damage per second, and a growth curve prices each level as a power of a ratio.

blocks.text: Each calculation answers a different question, namely how strong one swing is, how long a fight lasts and how fast the cost of progress rises. Sources and sinks connect them, because the coins a fight pays out have to be balanced against the coins a shop takes back, and any figure has to be checked by play before it is trusted.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns from calculation to testing, and shows how to build a cheap prototype and run a playtest that answers a specific question.

lessons.title: Prototyping and playtesting

lead.text: A designer of a card game wants to know whether the coins players earn will pile up or run out, and a handful of paper cards and some tokens will answer the question in ten minutes. A cheap, quick version built to answer a single design question is called a **prototype**, and its virtue is that it contains only what the question needs.

Give each player 10 coins, deal a card each round for five rounds, and record after each round whether the coins are piling up or running out. Paper suits rules and economies especially well, because what is being tested is the numbers and not how the game looks.

afterFigure.text: A card cost of 3 against an income of 2 leaves the player 1 coin worse off each round, and after five rounds 5 coins are left, while with a cost of 1 the same player gains a coin a round. **One cheap test settles the question** before any code exists.

reveal.text: Counting through the rounds is the same operation the designer would do with cards, and it shows the direction of the economy immediately.

lead.text: A **playtest** is a session in which players who have never seen the game try it while the designer watches. Two habits make it work. The first is to stay silent, because if the designer explains how to open the door, the test no longer shows whether a new player would have found it. The second is to watch what players do and not to ask whether they liked it, because players are polite, while a player who stops for forty seconds in front of a door has told you something exact.
A playtest question therefore has to be one that watching can answer, and the best are specific and measurable, such as whether players find the exit of the first room within two minutes.

reveal.text: Each of the other questions asks the player for an opinion or asks something that no single session could settle.
The next screen sets the steps side by side, and shows why the step that loses the most players need not be the one that keeps the smallest share.

lead.text: A playtest of six people shows a few things in great detail. To see where thousands of players struggle, a game logs events as they happen, such as starting the tutorial or beating a level, and the log is called **telemetry**. Counting how many players reach each logged step makes a **funnel**. Suppose 200 players start, 150 finish the tutorial, 90 beat level 1 and 45 beat level 2.

Counts alone mislead. The tutorial loses 50 players, level 1 loses 60 and level 2 loses 45, so level 1 looks like the worst step. Level 2 had only 90 players to begin with, however, and lost half of them. Dividing the players who got through a step by the players who *reached* it gives 75 percent for the tutorial, 60 percent for level 1 and 50 percent for level 2, and **the step that keeps the smallest share is level 2**.

afterFigure.text: Neither is complete alone: the counts say how many people a fix would help, and the shares say where the step itself is failing.

steps.headline: Using the funnel of 200, 150, 90 and 45 players, find the share kept at each of the three steps.

workedSteps.text: For the tutorial, the players who reached it are the 200 who started, and 150 got through it.
For level 1 the players who reached it are the 150 who finished the tutorial. Say what the denominator at any step is, in one word.
This gives 60 percent for level 1, and for level 2, where 90 reached it and 45 got through, 50 percent. The lowest share marks the step to look at first.

steps.headline: Read a second funnel: 300 players started, 240 finished the tutorial and 180 beat level 1.

workedSteps.text: The tutorial kept 240 of the 300 players who reached it.
Level 1 was reached by the 240 who finished the tutorial, and 180 of them beat it. Work out the share kept at level 1, as a percentage.

lead.text: The designer finds the weakest step, changes something about it, and tests again with a new group. If three things change at once and the share improves, no one can tell which change was responsible.

lessons.orientation: Build a prototype to answer one question, run a playtest that watches rather than asks, and read a funnel.
lessons.nextAction: Write a fixed-timestep game loop and say what the accumulator does.

blocks.text: Every design decision is a prediction about how people will play, such as that the coins earned in a card game will neither pile up nor run out, and a prediction is settled only by trying it. Building a whole game to try one is slow and costly, so designers build the smallest version that can answer a single question, called a prototype, which for a question about numbers like these can be nothing more than paper cards and tokens.

Questions about people need a different test, a playtest, in which players who have never seen the game are watched while they play. A game can also log what its players do, and this record, called telemetry, extends the same watching to thousands of them, with counts that show at which step they hesitate or leave.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to frame a question a playtest can answer, run a short paper test, and read a funnel by the share kept at each step.
intro.whyItMatters: Most design ideas fail in testing, so the designer who tests cheaply and early loses the least.

recap.keyIdea: A prototype answers one design question cheaply, a playtest watches players who do not know the game, and a telemetry funnel shows the share kept at each step.

blocks.text: The paper test showed a design question answered by counting, and the playtest showed a design question answered by watching. The funnel extends watching to thousands of players, as long as each step is measured against those who reached it, and a fix is tested by changing one thing and measuring again.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson begins the programming half of the course with the game loop, which keeps a simulation's results the same on a fast machine and a slow one.

lessons.title: The game loop and the fixed timestep

lead.text: A **game loop** repeats three jobs for as long as the game is running: it reads the player's input, updates the state of the world, and draws the result. In its simplest form it does so with no regard for time, going round again the instant it has finished.
A loop with no timing therefore makes a different game on every machine, so the passage of game time has to depend on the clock and not on how quickly the processor happens to work.

reveal.text: The result is twice the distance on a machine making 60 passes, from the same code, which is what a fix has to remove.

lead.text: The first fix is to measure how long each frame took, a quantity called **delta time**, and to move objects by speed × delta time. A ball moving at 300 pixels per second then moves 5 pixels in a frame of 1/60 of a second and 2.08 pixels in a frame of 1/144, and covers the same distance in a second on both. Because the step now varies with the frame time, this is called a **variable timestep**.

afterFigure.text: The steps are different sizes on different machines, so two machines running the same game can end up with slightly different results. A large step also causes **tunnelling**: in the figure a ball moving at 900 pixels per second meets a wall 10 pixels thick, and at 60 updates per second it moves 15 pixels at a time and can jump clean over the wall.

diagram.alt: A row of dots marking where a ball is after each update, with a wall 10 pixels thick. At 60 updates per second the dots are 15 pixels apart and none lands in the wall. At 144 updates per second they are 6.25 pixels apart and one does.
diagram.caption: A ball moving 900 pixels per second against a thin wall. Use the buttons to change the update rate.

reveal.text: The distance per update is now three times the thickness of the wall, so the ball is recorded on one side and then on the other.

lead.text: The fix is to make the simulation always advance by the same amount, the **fixed timestep**, such as 20 ms, which is 50 updates per second. Real frames still take whatever time they take, so the loop keeps a running total of the real time that has passed and not yet been simulated, called the **accumulator** or lag. Each frame it adds the frame's duration to the lag, and then, while the lag is at least one step, it runs an update and subtracts one step.

The update rate and the render rate are separate. A frame may run no updates, one, or several, but every update advances the world by exactly 20 ms, so a given sequence of inputs gives the same result on every machine. This design is described in Glenn Fiedler's article *Fix Your Timestep!*, which dates from 2004.

afterFigure.text: Take a frame of 70 ms with no lag waiting. The lag is 70 ms, so three updates run, which spends 60 ms and leaves 10 ms. The next frame takes 25 ms, which makes the lag 35 ms: one update runs and 15 ms remain. **Whatever the loop cannot spend stays in the accumulator**, as the figure shows.

diagram.alt: Bars for the accumulator. A frame of 70 ms with no lag runs 3 updates of 20 ms and leaves 10 ms. The next frame of 25 ms adds to that 10 ms to make 35 ms, which runs one update and leaves 15 ms.
diagram.caption: With a step of 20 ms, the accumulator spends whole steps and keeps the rest. Use the buttons to follow two frames.

reveal.text: A frame is not matched to an update, so a slow frame is followed by several updates, which together catch the simulation up.

steps.headline: Trace the accumulator for a step of 20 ms and frames of 30, 50 and 10 ms, starting with no lag.

workedSteps.text: In the first frame the lag becomes 30 ms. One whole step of 20 ms fits, so one update runs and 10 ms remain.
The second frame adds 50 ms to the 10 ms left over, so the lag is 60 ms and three updates run, leaving none. Say what the 10 ms carried between the two frames is called.
The third frame adds 10 ms, which is less than a step, so no update runs and 10 ms stay in the accumulator. The total over the three frames is 1 + 3 + 0 = 4 updates.

steps.headline: Trace the accumulator for a step of 20 ms and frames of 70, 25, 5 and 40 ms.

workedSteps.text: The first two frames are those of the figure: 3 updates leaving 10 ms, then 1 update leaving 15 ms.
Carry on through the frames of 5 ms and 40 ms, adding each to the remainder before spending whole steps. Work out how many updates run in all four frames.

lead.text: Because updates come in whole steps, the frame being drawn usually falls between two of them, and showing the latest update would make an object stutter. The remedy is to keep the previous state as well as the latest and to draw a blend: the leftover lag divided by the step gives a fraction from 0 to 1, and the object is drawn that fraction of the way from its previous position to its latest. This is called **interpolation**.

afterFigure.text: In the figure an object moved from x = 100 to x = 120 on the last update, so with 10 ms of lag the fraction is 0.5 and it is drawn at 110. The simulation itself stays on its fixed steps, and only the picture is placed between them.

diagram.alt: A line between a ball's previous position, 100, and its latest position, 120. A dot shows where the ball is drawn. With 10 ms of lag it is drawn at 110, and with 15 ms of lag at 115.
diagram.caption: Drawing a fraction of the way between the last two updates. Use the buttons to change the leftover lag.

reveal.text: The renderer reads the accumulator without changing it, so the picture moves smoothly while the simulation keeps its fixed steps.

lead.text: Suppose each update takes 25 ms of real time to compute but simulates only 20 ms. Every frame then spends more time catching up than the frame itself gave, the lag grows, and the loop never recovers. This is called the **spiral of death**.

afterFigure.text: The usual remedy is to cap the time a single frame may add to the lag, so that after a stall the loop skips the lost time. Fiedler's article caps it at 0.25 seconds, which is 250 ms, and with a step of 16 ms that allows at most 15 updates in a frame.

reveal.text: The loop gives up on the lost time instead of trying to catch up, and the cap guarantees the number of updates in any one frame.

lessons.orientation: Trace a fixed-timestep loop with an accumulator and explain what goes wrong with a variable step.
lessons.reviewLabel: The game loop and the fixed timestep
lessons.nextAction: Recognise a game object as a state machine and write its transition table.

blocks.text: A ball that moves 5 pixels each time the main loop of a game runs covers 300 pixels in a second when the loop runs 60 times per second, and it covers more on a machine that runs the loop faster. The code is the same everywhere, but the game is not, because the ball's speed has come to depend on how fast the processor happens to be, and a game that behaves differently on every machine cannot be tested, tuned or shared, while a competitive one cannot be fair.

Tying the speed of the game to a clock instead of to the processor means advancing the simulation in steps of a fixed length and spending the real time that has passed on whole steps, using a running total called the accumulator, so that a given sequence of inputs produces the same result on every machine.

diagram.alt: A bar for the distance a ball covers in one second. A loop running 60 times a second moves it 300 pixels. A loop running 144 times a second moves it 720 pixels.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to trace how many updates a fixed-timestep loop runs for a given sequence of frame times, and say why a variable step is not enough.
intro.whyItMatters: Every pattern in the rest of the course sits inside this loop, so its timing decides what the others can promise.

recap.keyIdea: A fixed-timestep loop advances the simulation by the same step every time, spending real time from an accumulator in whole steps, while the picture is drawn a fraction of the way between the last two updates.

blocks.text: A loop with no timing, or with a variable timestep, gives results that depend on the machine, so the simulation is advanced in fixed steps instead. The accumulator carries unspent real time between frames, interpolation hides the gap between steps in the picture, and a cap on the frame time stops a slow update from spiralling out of control.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at state machines, which give each object in the loop a clear set of states and the rules for moving between them.

lessons.title: State machines

reveal.text: Not every combination describes something a character can do, and the next screen sorts the real ones from the nonsense.

lead.text: A character that can jump, duck and dive is easily written with a flag for each: `isJumping`, `isDucking` and `isDiving`. The three flags together can hold 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 combinations, but only four of them describe something the character can be doing: none set, which is standing, and each flag alone. The other four, such as jumping and ducking at once, are nonsense, and every line of code that reads the flags has to cope with them or be sure they never arise. With each new behaviour the count doubles, so the code has to guard against more and more combinations that should not happen.

afterFigure.text: The remedy is to describe the character with a single variable that holds one of a fixed list of values, here standing, jumping, ducking and diving. An object that is in exactly one of a fixed set of states at any time, with rules for moving between them, is a **finite state machine**. **Every value of the variable is a real state**, so the impossible combinations are gone before any code is written.

diagram.alt: Two views. With three boolean flags there are eight combinations, of which four are real states and four are impossible. With one state variable there are four values, all of them real.

reveal.text: The number of combinations doubles with each flag, while the number of real states grows by only a few, so the flag approach gets worse as a character gains behaviours.

lead.text: Once a character has states, the rules for moving between them need writing down. A **transition** is a move from one state to another, **triggered by an event** such as pressing jump or touching the ground. The same information fits in a **transition table** with a row for each state and a column for each event, where each cell holds the state to move to.

A cell left empty means that the event does nothing in that state, so the machine stays where it is. Pressing jump while ducking, for instance, does nothing in this machine, and the table shows that explicitly instead of leaving it to a forgotten branch of code.

afterFigure.text: The diagram has six arrows, and the table has four rows and four columns, so sixteen cells, of which six hold a transition. The table makes gaps easy to see: **every state-and-event pair is either handled or visibly ignored**.

reveal.text: A table with this many cells is small enough to check by eye, which is much of its value.

steps.headline: Starting from standing, follow the events jump, duck, land and jump through the table of the four-state character.

workedSteps.text: From standing, the jump event gives the state jumping.
From jumping, the duck event gives diving, and the land event then gives standing.
The final jump takes standing to jumping, so the sequence ends there. Say what would have happened if an event had had no entry in the current row.

steps.headline: Starting from standing, follow the events jump, duck, release and land through the same table.

workedSteps.text: Jump takes standing to jumping, and duck takes jumping to diving.
Release has no entry in the diving row, so the state stays as it was. Then apply land and say which state the character ends in.

lead.text: A table says where to go, and the **state pattern** says what each state does while the machine is in it. Each state becomes its own object, with a method that handles input, a method that updates, and methods for moving in and out of it, and the character passes every input and every update to its current state object.

afterFigure.text: The **enter** method runs once when the machine moves into the state, to choose a sprite or start a timer. The **update** method runs on each tick of the game loop, and **exit** runs once on the way out, to clear what `enter` set up. Anything that must happen once at a transition therefore has a place that is not the update.

reveal.text: Putting setup in a method that runs once keeps the update free for the work that really has to repeat.

lead.text: Suppose the ground states are standing, walking, running and ducking, and each of them must jump when the jump event arrives, which in a flat machine is four identical arrows. A **hierarchical state machine** puts the four inside a parent state, on the ground, and gives the parent the jump transition once, so every substate inherits it.

afterFigure.text: A second extension is the **pushdown** stack of states. When the character is hit, the game pushes a stunned state onto the stack, and when the stun ends it pops it and returns to whatever state was underneath. Menus use the same idea: closing one brings back the game exactly as it was.

lessons.orientation: Draw a finite state machine, count its transitions, and say what the state pattern and hierarchical states add.
lessons.nextAction: Wrap an action as a command so it can be bound, queued, replayed and undone.

blocks.text: Suppose a character's behaviour is stored as one true-or-false flag for each thing it can do: `isJumping`, `isDucking` and `isDiving`. Each flag is easy to set and to read, but nothing in the flags themselves prevents `isJumping` and `isDucking` from both being true, and every rule about what may follow what, such as that a dive is possible only from a jump or that nothing is possible while the character is stunned, becomes another condition in each place that reads them.

A **state machine** avoids this by naming the states the character can really be in, listing the events that move it from one to another, and allowing exactly one state to be true at a time, so that the question whether the character is jumping and ducking at once never arises.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to count the combinations that flags allow, draw a small machine as a table, and trace a run of events through it.
intro.whyItMatters: State machines hold the behaviour of characters, menus and animations, and a flag that is easy to add is costly to remove.

recap.keyIdea: A finite state machine replaces a pile of flags with one state variable, whose transitions are listed in a table, and the state pattern, hierarchy and a pushdown stack keep that machine manageable as it grows.

blocks.text: Flags double the combinations with every new behaviour, whereas a state variable names only the states that can actually occur. A transition table lists every state and event pair, the state pattern gives each state a place for its code with enter, update and exit, and a parent state or a pushdown stack stops the machine from growing out of hand.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson wraps player actions as command objects, which allows keys to be rebound, actions to be queued and replayed, and moves to be undone.

lessons.title: Commands, input and undo

lead.text: The shortest way to handle input is to test for a key and act: if the key is Space, call the player's jump. A second input device then needs a second copy of the test, a player who wants to rebind the key must change the code, and nothing records that a jump happened, so there is nothing to undo or replay.

afterFigure.text: The remedy is to wrap each action as an object with a single method, `execute`, such as a `Jump` or a `MoveRight`. A request wrapped in this way is called a **command**, and the pattern is the **command pattern**. A **binding table**, with one row for each input and the command it triggers, then sits between the keys and the actions, so rebinding jump from Space to J changes one row of the table.

reveal.text: The other designs all store the key inside logic, so any change of key is a change to the code.

lead.text: A command does not care who issues it. An enemy's AI can create the very same Jump and MoveRight objects as the player's key presses, so one piece of code runs both, and the command takes the actor it should run on as a parameter.

afterFigure.text: If every command is stored with the frame at which it was issued, the list of commands is a complete description of a match, and feeding them to a fresh game at the same frames reproduces it. This works only if the game is deterministic, which is why the fixed timestep of the game loop lesson matters.

reveal.text: A small list of commands is easy to store and send, but it can be replayed only if the game responds to the same commands the same way each time.
The next screen follows the stack through the undos and then through a new command.

lead.text: To support undo, each command gains a second method, `undo`, that reverses what `execute` did, and the game keeps the executed commands in a list called the **undo stack**. Executing a command runs it and pushes it onto the stack. Undoing pops the most recent command, runs its `undo` method, and keeps it in a redo list so that it can be done again. After A, B, C and D, two undos reverse D and then C, leaving A and B applied.

afterFigure.text: The subtle point comes next. If the player now executes a new command E, the history is A, B, E, and the stack holds three commands. C and D can no longer be redone, because redoing them would apply them after E in a history that never contained them. **A new command clears the redo branch**, and forgetting this is a common source of bugs in editors and in games with rewind. The figure steps through the sequence.

diagram.alt: A row of command boxes. First A, B, C and D are all applied. After two undos A and B are applied and C and D are dashed, meaning they can be redone. After executing E the row is A, B, E and C and D are gone.
diagram.caption: The undo stack at three moments. Use the buttons to step through them.

reveal.text: The stack and the redo list are two parts of one history, and a new command ends the redo part.

steps.headline: Execute A, B and C, then undo twice, redo once, and execute D. Track which commands are applied.

workedSteps.text: After A, B and C the stack is A, B, C, all applied.
Two undos reverse C and then B, leaving A applied with B and C waiting to be redone. Redo then re-applies B, so A and B are applied and C is still waiting.
Executing D adds D after B and leaves C with no place in the history. Say what happens to C.

steps.headline: Execute A, B, C, D, E and F, undo three times, execute G, then undo once.

workedSteps.text: Three undos reverse F, E and D, leaving A, B and C applied.
workedSteps.math: A B C | D E F

workedSteps.text: Executing G discards D, E and F and adds G, so A, B, C and G are applied. One more undo reverses G. Work out how many commands are applied now.

lead.text: It is tempting to implement undo by saving a copy of the whole game before every action, but a game state can run to many megabytes. A move command can instead save the object's old position, and its undo puts the object back, so only the data that the command changed needs to be kept.

afterFigure.text: An action with random results must store the result that was drawn, or undoing and redoing it would give different outcomes.

reveal.text: Storing a small difference makes a long history practical, where a snapshot of the whole state after each move would not be.

lessons.orientation: Wrap an action as a command, bind inputs through a table, and trace an undo stack.
lessons.nextAction: Compose game objects from components and compare array-of-structs with struct-of-arrays layouts.

blocks.text: Take the simplest way of handling input: if the key pressed is Space, the player jumps. Once that line has run, nothing remains of what happened except its effect, so the game cannot undo the jump, replay it later or let an enemy make the same jump, and moving jump to another key means finding every place where the key is tested.

Wrapping each action in an object removes those limits, because an object can be kept after it has run, handed to a different caller and asked to reverse itself. A key can then be tied to a different object without touching the code that does the work, and the arrangement is known as the command pattern.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to explain how a binding table decouples input from logic, and trace an undo stack through undo and a new command.
intro.whyItMatters: Rebinding, replays and undo all become easy once an action is an object, and nearly impossible when it is a line of code inside an input handler.

recap.keyIdea: A command wraps an action as an object, so a binding table can map inputs to commands, an undo stack can reverse them, and a new command discards the redo branch.

blocks.text: Because each action is an object, the same Jump can be issued by a key, an AI or a recording, and the history of commands is what undo and replay work from. Each command stores only what it needs to reverse itself, and the redo branch ends at the first new command.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to components, which build game objects from parts instead of deep inheritance, and compares ways of laying data out in memory.

lessons.title: Components and data layout

reveal.text: The number is more than the three traits suggest, and the next screen shows what grows while the traits only increase by one.

lead.text: Inheritance suggests a family tree of classes, with a `Monster` at the top and a `Flier`, a `Swimmer` and a `Poisoner` beneath it. The tree fails when traits combine: three independent traits need 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 classes, and each trait added doubles the count.

afterFigure.text: The **component pattern** replaces the tree with parts. An **entity** is a plain object that owns a list of **components**, each handling one concern such as position, drawing, flying or poison. A monster that flies and poisons simply holds those two components, and one that swims holds a swimming component instead. **Adding a trait means writing one component**, and all the rare combinations come free.

diagram.alt: Two views of monsters with three optional traits. By inheritance there are eight classes. With components, one monster entity holds a list of parts, and a monster that flies and poisons holds the flies and poison components and not the swims component.

reveal.text: Each trait multiplies the classes by two, whereas the component design needs only one more part.

lead.text: The pattern can be pushed further. In an **entity component system**, an entity is nothing but an id. A component is plain data with no behaviour, stored with all the other components of its type, so there is one collection of positions, one of velocities and one of health values, each indexed by entity id. The behaviour sits in **systems**, which are functions that loop over every entity having the components they need. A movement system, for example, visits every entity with both a position and a velocity and adds the one to the other.

afterFigure.text: In the figure, five entities have different mixes of components. A crate has position and health but cannot move, a bullet has position and velocity but no health, and entity 3, a signpost, has only a position. The movement system needs both position and velocity, so it skips entities 1 and 3 and processes entities 0, 2 and 4, which is **three of the five**. An entity is changed by adding or removing a component, and the systems pick it up without any change to their code.

reveal.text: Keeping behaviour out of components and entities is what lets one system treat all matching entities the same way.

lead.text: There is a second reason for storing components in arrays, and it comes from the hardware. A processor does not fetch single bytes from memory. It fetches a block called a **cache line**, commonly 64 bytes, and keeps it close at hand, so that reading anything in the same block afterwards is fast. A position of three floats of 4 bytes each takes 12 bytes, and 64 ÷ 12 = 5.33, so a line holds 5 whole positions.

afterFigure.text: If positions are packed in an array, one fetch brings in five of them and the next five are in the next line, as the figure shows. If each position sits inside a different object somewhere on the heap, each fetch brings in 64 bytes of which only 12 are wanted, and the processor waits for memory far more often. This property of keeping related data close together is called **data locality**, and it is the reason a loop over an array is faster than a chase through pointers.

reveal.text: Whole records only: a record that straddles the end of a line is split across two fetches.

steps.headline: Count the 64-byte cache lines needed to read 640 packed positions of 12 bytes each.

workedSteps.text: The array holds 640 positions of 12 bytes each, so the total size comes first.
The processor reads memory in blocks of one fixed size. Name that block, whose size is 64 bytes.
Dividing gives 120 lines for the packed array. If every position were in a line of its own, the worst case would be one line for each position, which is 640.

steps.headline: A game stores 800 velocities of 2 floats each, packed in one array, and the processor reads them in 64-byte lines.

workedSteps.text: A velocity is 2 floats of 4 bytes each, which is 8 bytes, so 800 of them take 6400 bytes.
Now divide the size of the array by the size of a cache line, and work out how many lines the array occupies.

lead.text: Locality depends on which data a loop needs. If each entity is a record holding its position, velocity, health and a good deal else, the array of such records is an **array of structs**. A movement system that wants only position and velocity still pulls the whole record through the cache. The alternative is a **struct of arrays**, with one array of positions, one of velocities and so on, so that the movement system reads two arrays and nothing else.

afterFigure.text: Take 1000 entities with 64-byte records, of which position and velocity use 12 + 12 = 24 bytes. Reading whole records touches 1000 lines, and reading separate arrays touches 1000 × 24 ÷ 64 = 375 lines. The gain depends on the shape of the work: **when only a few entities share a component, or the loop needs most of each record, the saving is small**.

lessons.orientation: Choose composition over inheritance and count cache lines for packed and scattered data.
lessons.nextAction: Decouple a sender from its receivers with observers and an event queue, and trace a ring buffer.

blocks.text: A monster that flies and a monster that poisons are each easy to write as a class. A monster that does both is harder, because it belongs under neither class, so code has to be copied from one into the other, or a shared ancestor invented that has no natural meaning, and the same trouble returns with every new combination of traits.

Game programmers instead build a monster from parts, giving it a component for each thing it can do, and in the entity component system those parts become plain data held in arrays. Storing them that way also suits the processor, which reads memory in blocks and so finds packed data far cheaper to fetch than objects scattered across the heap.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to choose between inheritance and composition for a set of traits, and count the cache lines that packed and scattered data need.
intro.whyItMatters: A game with hundreds of kinds of object stays workable only if new kinds are cheap to make, which composition supports and inheritance does not.

recap.keyIdea: A component design builds an entity from independent parts, an entity component system stores those parts as plain data in arrays that systems loop over, and packed data is fetched in fewer 64-byte cache lines.

blocks.text: Inheritance multiplies classes with each independent trait, while composition adds one part. Keeping the parts as arrays also lets a processor fetch them in whole cache lines, and the saving is greatest when many entities share the same components and a system needs only some of their data.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson shows how one part of a game can tell others that something has happened without knowing who is listening, using observers and event queues.

lessons.title: Events and queues

lead.text: The damage code of a game decides that the player has died. Many systems care: the achievements system counts deaths, the audio plays a sound, and the interface shows a message. The direct way to handle this is for the damage code to call each of those systems itself, and it works until a fourth system is added, or until someone asks why the physics and damage code has to know about trophies at all.

afterFigure.text: The **observer pattern** removes the knowledge. The thing that has something to announce, called the **subject**, keeps a list of **listeners**, and when the event happens it walks the list and notifies each one. Each system registers itself, and the damage code never names them, so adding a system means adding a listener and changing nothing else. **The subject knows that listeners exist and not what they do**.

diagram.alt: Two wiring diagrams. In the first, the damage code calls the achievements, audio and interface systems directly. In the second it notifies a list of listeners, and the three systems have registered themselves in that list.
diagram.caption: The same player-died event, wired two ways. Use the buttons to compare them.

reveal.text: A call of that length stalls the subject for several frames, and the next screen sets out when that matters and what else can go wrong.

lead.text: The observer pattern has two weaknesses. The first is that notification is **synchronous**: the subject calls each listener and waits for it to return before carrying on, so if three listeners take 2, 4 and 50 ms, the damage code waits for all of them, 56 ms in total.

afterFigure.text: The second weakness is the lapsed listener: an object that has been destroyed but never unregistered stays on the list and is still called, which wastes time and can crash the game. Listeners must be removed when they are destroyed.

reveal.text: Each wasted call is small, but the list grows with every object that is destroyed without being removed.

lead.text: An **event queue** answers the cost of synchronous calls. The sender adds a small record of the event to a queue and carries on at once, and at a chosen point in the game loop, such as the start of the update, the game takes events from the queue and delivers them to the listeners.

afterFigure.text: The sender no longer waits, and the game can choose how much work to do per frame. The cost is that a listener sees the event a little later than it happened, and a queue that fills faster than it is emptied has to decide what to do with the overflow.

reveal.text: The slow work still has to be done, but with the queue it no longer holds up the code that raised the event.

lead.text: A queue could be stored in a list that grows and shrinks, but allocating memory in the middle of a game is costly. A **ring buffer** uses a fixed array instead and two indices. The **tail** marks the slot where the next event will be written, and the **head** marks the slot from which the next event will be read. An enqueue writes at the tail and then moves the tail on by one, and a dequeue reads at the head and moves the head on by one. Past the last slot the index returns to the first, so with capacity 4 the slots are used in the order 0, 1, 2, 3, 0, 1 and so on.

afterFigure.text: The wrap is written with the **modulo** operation, which gives the remainder after division: tail = (tail + 1) mod capacity. In the figure the tail starts at 3. The first enqueue sets it to (3 + 1) mod 4 = 0, and the second to (0 + 1) mod 4 = 1. Because head and tail can meet whether the buffer is empty or full, implementations also keep a count of the events waiting.

diagram.alt: A ring of four numbered slots, 0 to 3, with a head marker for the next read and a tail marker for the next write. Slot 2 holds an event and the tail is at 3. After one more event is written the tail wraps to 0, and after another it is at 1.
diagram.caption: Capacity 4. Each enqueue writes at the tail and moves it on by one, wrapping to 0 after 3. Use the buttons to step through two enqueues.

reveal.text: The tail never reaches 4, and the same rule gives the next slot from every position.

steps.headline: A ring buffer has capacity 5 and its tail starts at 2. Follow the tail through four enqueues.

workedSteps.text: The first enqueue writes at slot 2 and moves the tail on to the next slot.
The second gives 4, and at the third the index would reach 5, so the wrap is needed. Name the operation that brings it back to 0.
After the fourth enqueue the tail has moved on once more, so it ends at slot 1.

steps.headline: A ring buffer has capacity 6 and its tail starts at 4. Follow the tail through five enqueues.

workedSteps.text: The first enqueue moves the tail to 5, and the second wraps it to 0.
Three more enqueues move it on one slot each. Work out the tail index after all five enqueues.

reveal.text: Moving the same three handlers behind a queue takes this wait out of the damage code, though the handlers still have to run somewhere.

lessons.orientation: Decouple a sender from its receivers with observers and event queues, and trace a ring buffer.
lessons.nextAction: Reuse objects with a pool and share data with the flyweight pattern.

blocks.text: When the player dies, four systems need to know: the audio plays a sound, the interface shows a message, the achievements count the death and the analytics log it. The simplest code calls all four from the few lines in the damage calculation that decide the player has died, which makes that function depend on every one of them, so that adding a fifth system means editing it again and testing it means having all four present.

The way out is to let the damage code announce that the player has died and leave the other systems to listen for it. An announcement passed straight to every system that has asked to hear it is the observer pattern, while one stored to be delivered later is an event queue, and the choice between them depends on how long a listener takes and when its work should be done.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say when an observer is enough and when a queue is better, and trace a ring buffer's tail through a series of enqueues.
intro.whyItMatters: Games are made of systems that must stay independent, and events are how they talk without knowing about each other.

recap.keyIdea: An observer lets a subject notify listeners without knowing them, an event queue also separates the two in time, and a ring buffer is a fixed array whose index wraps with modulo.

blocks.text: The observer pattern removes the subject's knowledge of its listeners, but notification is synchronous, so a slow or lapsed listener hurts the subject. A queue holds events until the game chooses to handle them, and a ring buffer implements it in a fixed array whose indices wrap.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at objects that are created and destroyed constantly, and shows how a pool reuses them and how a flyweight shares data between them.

lessons.title: Object pools and flyweights

lead.text: A shooter fires many bullets each second, and the simple approach creates a bullet object when the trigger is pulled and frees it when the bullet hits something. Asking the system for memory takes time, and the deeper problem is that objects of different sizes are created and freed in no particular order, so the free memory gets broken into small gaps.

afterFigure.text: This is **fragmentation**. In the figure, 5 of the 12 blocks are free, yet the longest run of free blocks is only 2, so an object that needs 3 blocks in a row cannot be placed.

diagram.alt: A strip of twelve memory blocks. In the first view some are used and five are free but scattered, so the longest free run is two blocks. In the second, a pool reserves twelve equal slots, some active and some free, and reuses them.
