text-anchor="middle">bullet</text><text class="t" x="320" y="230" text-anchor="middle">All slots are the same size and sit in one block.</text><text class="t" x="320" y="262" text-anchor="middle">A bullet that ends makes its slot free again, and the next</text><text class="t" x="320" y="288" text-anchor="middle">bullet takes it, so no gaps are ever left behind.</text></svg>

reveal.text: A fixed number of slots is the point of the idea and also its limit, which the next screen takes up.

lead.text: An **object pool** creates a fixed number of objects when the game starts, and hands them out as they are needed. Each slot has a flag saying whether it is active, or the pool keeps a **free list**, a list of the slots that are free. Firing a bullet takes a slot from the free list and marks it active, and when the bullet ends its slot goes back on the list. No memory is requested during play, and since every slot has the same size no gaps appear.

afterFigure.text: When every slot is taken the game has to choose: **refuse** the new request, **overwrite the oldest** active object, or **grow** the pool, which brings back the allocation the pool was meant to avoid.

diagram.alt: A pool of three bullet slots shown at three moments. At first all are free. Then all three are active and a fourth shot is refused. Then the bullet in slot 1 expires and the next shot can take it.
diagram.caption: A pool of 3 slots with a free list. Use the buttons to follow it.

reveal.text: Expired bullets return their slots at once, so what matters is the number of slots free when the new shots begin.

lead.text: Memory can also be saved by not copying what is the same. A forest of 10,000 trees might use one tree mesh of 20,000 bytes. If each tree object carries its own copy of the mesh together with its 12 bytes of position, the forest takes 10,000 × (20,000 + 12) = 200,120,000 bytes, about 200 megabytes, almost all of it the same mesh stored again and again.

afterFigure.text: The **flyweight pattern** keeps one copy of the shared data and has every tree refer to it. The forest then costs 20,000 + 10,000 × 12 = 140,000 bytes, which is about 1,430 times less. The shared data is called the **intrinsic state**, because it belongs to the kind of tree and is the same for every one. What differs between trees, such as the position, is **extrinsic state**, and each instance keeps its own.

diagram.alt: Two ways of storing trees. In the first every tree holds its own 20,000-byte mesh and 12 bytes of position, totalling 200,120,000 bytes for 10,000 trees. In the second all trees point to one shared mesh and keep only their position, totalling 140,000 bytes.
diagram.caption: Sharing the data that never changes. Use the buttons to compare the two.

reveal.text: The mesh is paid for once, and each extra tree costs only its own 12 bytes.

steps.headline: A field has 5,000 rocks. The shared rock mesh is 8,000 bytes, and each rock keeps 16 bytes of position and rotation. Find the memory with and without sharing.

workedSteps.text: Without sharing, each rock carries the mesh and its own 16 bytes, so every rock costs 8,016 bytes.
With sharing the mesh is stored once. Say what the data that is the same for every rock is called.
The shared total is 8,000 + 80,000 = 88,000 bytes, which saves 40,080,000 − 88,000 = 39,992,000 bytes.

steps.headline: A game has 2,000 enemies that share one 50,000-byte sprite, and each enemy keeps 20 bytes of its own state.

workedSteps.text: The sprite is intrinsic state, stored once, and the 20 bytes are extrinsic state, stored for each enemy.
Now add the shared sprite to the per-enemy state of all the enemies, and work out the total memory in bytes.

lead.text: A piece of data may be shared only if every instance would have held the same value and no instance ever changes it. A tree's mesh passes, while its position and its current wind sway fail, and if the sway were put inside the shared mesh, every tree would sway in step. **Per-instance state stays outside the flyweight.**

afterFigure.text: A pool reserves its memory before it is needed, and a flyweight adds a level of indirection, so both are worth their cost only when many objects are created and destroyed in play, or when many objects share large data.

reveal.text: Each of the others is different for every tree, so sharing it would make the trees identical in that respect.
The shared part stays at 20,000 bytes however many trees there are, and it is the per-tree part that grows.

lessons.orientation: Trace an object pool and compute the memory a flyweight saves.
lessons.nextAction: Use a uniform grid to cut collision checks and compute cell indices and pair counts.

blocks.text: A game can be unable to create an object even though the total amount of free memory is more than enough, because the free memory is scattered in gaps and none of them is large enough. The gaps appear when a game creates and frees small objects in no particular order, as a shooter does with every bullet it fires and every bullet that lands, and each request for memory also costs a little time.

A pool avoids the requests altogether by creating a fixed set of objects once and reusing them, and a flyweight attacks a different cost, the memory taken by many objects that each hold a copy of the same data, by keeping a single copy that they all share.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to trace a pool of slots through fire and expire events, and compute the memory a shared flyweight saves.
intro.whyItMatters: Memory is limited and slow to request on many devices, so a game that churns through objects needs a plan for reusing them.

recap.keyIdea: A pool reuses a fixed set of objects to avoid allocation and fragmentation, and a flyweight stores data that is identical for every instance once and keeps only the differences with each instance.

blocks.text: The pool trades memory reserved in advance for the absence of allocation and gaps, and it needs a rule for when it is full. The flyweight trades a little indirection for a large saving, provided that only intrinsic data is shared and every instance keeps its own extrinsic data.

recap.nextHook: The last lesson counts the collision checks a world needs, and shows how a grid cuts them by testing only objects that are close together.

lessons.title: Spatial partitioning

reveal.text: Counting works for five entities but not for a thousand, and the next screen gives the rule that does.

lead.text: The simplest way to find which entities collide is to test every pair. Each of n entities pairs with n − 1 others, which makes n × (n − 1) pairings, but each pair appears twice in that count, once from each end, so the number of distinct tests is n(n − 1) ÷ 2. With 4 entities that is 6 tests, with 5 it is 10, and with 6 it is 15.

afterFigure.text: A thousand entities need 1000 × 999 ÷ 2 = 499,500 tests every frame, nearly 30 million tests a second at 60 frames per second. Since **the count grows with the square of the number of entities**, doubling the crowd makes the work almost four times as large.

diagram.alt: Entities drawn as dots with a line for every pair. Four entities have 6 pairs, five have 10 and six have 15.
diagram.caption: Every pair of entities is one collision test. Use the buttons to add entities and count the lines.

reveal.text: Doubling 100 entities to 200 raises the count from 4,950 to nearly four times that, which is why the formula matters.

lead.text: Spatial partitioning keeps entities sorted by where they are, so that only nearby ones are compared. The simplest form is a **uniform grid**. The world is divided into equal square cells, and an entity is stored in the cell that holds its position. The cell is found by dividing each coordinate by the cell size and rounding down: cell column = floor(x ÷ cell size), and cell row = floor(y ÷ cell size). The result is called the **cell index**.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows a world of 1,000 by 1,000 units with 100-unit cells, so it has 10 × 10 = 100 cells. The entity at (250, 730) has column floor(2.5) = 2 and row floor(7.3) = 7, so it sits in cell (2, 7), with rows counted from the top. Entities are stored per cell, so a test needs only the entities of a few cells instead of the whole world. A position exactly on a boundary, such as x = 300, belongs to the cell that starts there.

reveal.text: The same rule applied to y gives the row, and together they name the cell.

steps.headline: Find the cell of an entity at (480, 90) in a grid of 100-unit cells.

workedSteps.text: The column comes from dividing x by the cell size and rounding down.
The quotient 4.8 has a fractional part. Name the operation that turns it into a whole cell index.
The row comes the same way from y, so the entity is in cell column 4, row 0.

steps.headline: Find the cell of an entity at (730, 250) in a grid of 50-unit cells.

workedSteps.text: The row comes from y: 250 ÷ 50 is exactly 5, so the row is 5.
The column comes from x in the same way. Divide 730 by 50, round down, and give the column index.

lead.text: An entity near the edge of its cell can overlap an entity in the next one, so a collision check looks at the entity's own cell and the eight cells around it, which is 9 cells in all. Moving entities are handled by recomputing the cell index each frame.

afterFigure.text: A cell size close to the largest entity works well. A uniform grid also assumes the entities are spread evenly, and when they crowd into one region, a **quadtree** splits any square holding too many entities into four smaller squares, again and again, and leaves empty areas whole. A BSP tree divides the world with planes in a similar hierarchical way.

diagram.alt: A square world with thirteen entities, most of them crowded in the top left corner. In the first view an even grid divides it. In the second, a quadtree splits the crowded top-left region into smaller and smaller squares and leaves the empty regions whole.

reveal.text: The number of cells shows how finely the world is divided, and it falls quickly as the cells grow.
A cell size close to the entities' size is a better compromise than either extreme.
The saving comes from skipping every pair that is far apart, and it grows as the world gets larger while the cells stay the same size.

lessons.orientation: Count the collision checks a world needs and use a uniform grid to cut them.
lessons.nextAction: You can now describe a game's design with MDA and core loops, tune its numbers, trace a fixed-timestep loop, and choose and trace the patterns that structure it.

blocks.text: Every frame a game must decide which of its entities touch, and the obvious method, which is to test each one against every other, needs 499,500 tests for a thousand entities, repeated sixty times a second. Most of those tests compare things on opposite sides of the world, and no amount of faster code makes the count grow any more slowly as the crowd gets larger.

Spatial partitioning avoids the pointless tests by keeping entities sorted by where they are, so that each entity is compared only with those nearby. A grid of equal cells is the simplest way to do it, and a tree that splits crowded areas into smaller squares handles worlds where the entities bunch together.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to count pairwise tests, compute the cell an entity falls in, and say what a grid and a quadtree each save.
intro.whyItMatters: Collision and nearest-neighbour queries are among the heaviest work in a game, and partitioning is the standard way to keep them affordable.

recap.keyIdea: Testing every pair takes n(n − 1) ÷ 2 checks, a uniform grid files each entity under floor(position ÷ cell size) in each axis so that only its own and neighbouring cells need checking, and a quadtree does the same for crowds that are uneven.

blocks.text: The all-pairs count grows with the square of the number of entities, so a game keeps entities sorted by position. A uniform grid is the simplest sorting, with its cell found by division and rounding down, and a quadtree refines the same idea where entities crowd together.

questions.prompt: Each piece covers 4 squares and a row holds 10. How many pieces fill four complete rows exactly, with no gaps?
hints: Count the squares in four rows first.
Four rows of ten squares is a total, not a number of pieces.
Divide the total by the squares in one piece.
questions.onCorrect: Forty squares need ten pieces, but a row of ten is not a multiple of four, so pieces must straddle rows and perfect fits are rare.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four rows of 10 squares make 40 squares, and 40 ÷ 4 = 10 pieces.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of rows. Each piece covers four squares, so count the squares in the rows first.
That multiplies the rows by the squares in a piece. Count the squares in the four rows, then see how many pieces of four squares they hold.

questions.prompt: A Tetris player lays every S-shaped piece flat against the bottom of the pile rather than standing it on end, to avoid leaving a hole. In MDA, which layer does this behaviour belong to?
hints: Does any rule of the game say which way an S-shaped piece should lie?
Is the way the piece is laid something the game does, something the player does, or something the player feels?
questions.onCorrect: No rule asks for it. Players adopt the habit because a buried hole cannot be cleared until the rows above it have gone.

misconceptions.feedback: A mechanic is a rule or a piece of data that a program could check, and no rule of Tetris says which way a piece should lie. The habit appears only when people play.
An aesthetic is a feeling the player has, such as challenge. Laying a piece flat is something the player does, and any feeling it produces is a separate matter.

questions.prompt: In a racing game, which of these statements describes an aesthetic?
hints: An aesthetic is something the player feels.
Rules and measurements are written by the designer.
questions.onCorrect: The thrill is an emotional response. The grip limit and track length are rules and data, and early braking is behaviour.

acceptedIdeas: The thrill of staying just ahead of a rival.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The thrill of staying just ahead of a rival.

choices.label: Players brake early before bends to protect their lead.
The thrill of staying just ahead of a rival.
The car loses grip above 120 km/h.

misconceptions.feedback: A grip limit is a rule with a number in it, so it is a mechanic.
Early braking is behaviour that emerges from the rules, so it is a dynamic.
The length of the track is data that a program holds, so it belongs with the mechanics.

questions.prompt: In an action, feedback and reward cycle, what is the name for the part that shows the player what their action just did?
hints: It is the second of the three words.
questions.onCorrect: Feedback is what makes the action readable, and the reward gives the player a reason to repeat it.

questions.prompt: In the platformer loop each pass collects one coin worth 10 points, and the score starts at 0. What is the score after 6 passes?
hints: Each pass changes the state by the same amount.
Add 10 once for every pass.
Multiply the passes by the points per pass.
questions.onCorrect: The score is the changed state each pass leaves behind, which is why the loop never starts from exactly the same situation twice.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each pass adds 10 points, so after 6 passes the score is 6 × 10 = 60.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the score after one pass. The loop repeats, and each pass adds 10 more.
That adds the numbers instead of multiplying them. Six passes of 10 points each is 6 × 10.

questions.prompt: A level takes 90 seconds, and the player unlocks a new ability after every 5 levels. How many minutes of play pass between unlocks?
hints: Find the time for five levels in seconds.
Divide by 60 to turn seconds into minutes.
5 × 90 = 450 seconds.
questions.onCorrect: The unlock loop is about 90 times longer than the 5-second core loop, which is why it can only be a reason to keep playing and not the thing the player does most often.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 5 levels × 90 seconds = 450 seconds, and 450 ÷ 60 = 7.5 minutes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time in seconds. The question asks for minutes, so divide by 60.
That is the length of one level in minutes. The unlock comes after five of them.

questions.prompt: 'Players hoard a power-up until the last moment.' In MDA, this is a:
hints: Is it a rule, or something players do because of the rules?
questions.onCorrect: Hoarding is emergent behaviour: the rules only set the power-up's effect and cost.

misconceptions.feedback: The rule is what the power-up does. Hoarding it is a choice players make because of that rule.
An aesthetic is a feeling. Hoarding is an action players take.
An asset is something the game contains, such as a sound or a model. Hoarding is behaviour.

questions.prompt: A game has a stamina bar. Which of these statements describes a mechanic?
hints: A mechanic is a rule or a piece of data that a program could check.
questions.onCorrect: It is a rule with a number in it, which a program can check on every jump.

misconceptions.feedback: Saving stamina for a particular fight is behaviour that appears when people play, which makes it a dynamic. No rule asks players to do it.
Tension is a feeling the player has, so it is an aesthetic. A rule can make the feeling more likely but cannot state it.

choices.label: Players save their stamina for the boss fight.
The tension of running low on stamina in mid-air.

questions.prompt: The short action, feedback and reward cycle a player repeats most often is the ___ loop.
hints: It is the loop at the centre.
questions.onCorrect: Outer loops wrap around it and decide why the player repeats it.

questions.prompt: A game runs at 60 frames per second, so the screen is redrawn sixty times in each second. About how long does one frame last?
hints: A frame is one sixtieth of a second.
One second is 1000 milliseconds, shared out among the sixty frames.
questions.onCorrect: A frame is one sixtieth of a second, which is 16.7 ms to one decimal place. At 30 frames per second a frame lasts twice as long, 33.3 ms, and at 120 half as long, 8.3 ms.

misconceptions.feedback: A second holds 1000 milliseconds, and those are shared among sixty frames. Each frame gets about ten times more than 1.7 milliseconds.
Sixty is the number of frames in a second, not the length of one. At 60 milliseconds a frame, only about 17 frames would fit in a second.
At 170 milliseconds a frame, only about six frames would fit in a second, far fewer than sixty.

questions.prompt: At 60 frames per second, how many whole frames fit in 150 ms?
hints: Divide the delay by the length of one frame.
Use the frame length of 16.7 ms.
150 ÷ 16.7 is very close to a whole number.
questions.onCorrect: So a delay of 150 ms at 60 frames per second is exactly nine frames, half as many again as the six in 100 ms.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A frame lasts 1000 ÷ 60 ms, and 150 ÷ (1000 ÷ 60) = 9.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the delay by the frame rate. Divide it by the length of one frame instead.
That multiplies instead of dividing. A delay of 150 ms holds fewer frames than ms.

questions.prompt: To turn a delay counted in frames into milliseconds, do you multiply or divide the frame count by the length of a frame? Answer with one word.
hints: Four frames of 16.7 ms each are four lots of 16.7 ms.
questions.onCorrect: Frames times frame length gives milliseconds, and the reverse conversion divides.

misconceptions.feedback: Dividing turns milliseconds into frames. Going from frames to milliseconds is the reverse.

questions.prompt: At 60 frames per second a hit pauses the game for 2 frames. How long is the pause in milliseconds, to one decimal place?
hints: Find the length of one frame first.
Frames to milliseconds means multiplying by the frame length.
Two frames are two lots of 16.67 ms.
questions.onCorrect: About a thirtieth of a second is enough to make a blow feel heavier without stopping the game in any way a player would call a pause.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each frame lasts 1000 ÷ 60 = 16.67 ms, so two frames last 33.3 ms.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one frame. The pause lasts two.
That divides the frame rate by the frames in the pause. Multiply the frames by the length of one frame instead.

questions.prompt: A sword hit sets off a large flash that covers the enemy, so the player cannot see its next move. This is a problem of:
hints: Which of the four words is about being able to read the screen?
questions.onCorrect: The response arrives on time, but it hides the state the player needs, so extra effects can make a game worse.

misconceptions.feedback: Latency is a delay between input and response. Here the response comes on time and is the trouble.
Balance is about numbers such as damage and cost, and nothing here concerns them.
Pooling is a way of reusing objects. It has nothing to do with what the player can see.

questions.prompt: What is the grace period called during which a jump is still accepted just after the player has run off a ledge?
hints: It is named after a cartoon animal that hangs in the air after leaving a cliff.
questions.onCorrect: The window is usually a handful of frames, so the player is forgiven for a press that was a moment late.

questions.prompt: A control responds 3 frames after the press. At 30 frames per second this delay is how many milliseconds longer than at 60 frames per second?
hints: Work out the delay in milliseconds at each frame rate.
A frame is longer at the lower frame rate.
Subtract the shorter delay from the longer one.
questions.onCorrect: The same code delay costs twice as much real time at half the frame rate, so response targets are better set in milliseconds.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At 30 fps three frames last 3 × 33.3 = 100 ms, at 60 fps they last 3 × 16.7 = 50 ms, and the difference is 50 ms.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the delay at 30 frames per second alone. The question asks for the difference between the two delays.
That is the delay in frames, and it is the same at both rates. Compare the times those frames take.

questions.prompt: At 30 frames per second, how long is one frame in milliseconds, rounded to one decimal place?
hints: Frame time is one second divided into equal frames.
Convert one second to milliseconds first.
Divide 1000 ms by the frames in a second.
questions.onCorrect: Halving the frame rate doubles the frame length, which is why the same frame count means a longer wait.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One frame lasts 1000 ÷ 30 = 33.33 ms, which rounds to 33.3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of frames in a second. The question asks for the length of one of them.
That is the length in seconds. The question asks for milliseconds.

questions.prompt: At 60 frames per second, a hit pauses the game for 3 frames. How long is the pause in milliseconds?
hints: Find the length of one frame first.
A frame lasts 1000 ÷ 60 ms.
Multiply the length of one frame by the frames in the pause.
questions.onCorrect: Fifty ms is a twentieth of a second, a pause that reads as weight and not as a stall.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three frames of 1000 ÷ 60 ms each last 50 ms.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one frame. The pause lasts three.
That multiplies the frame rate by the frames in the pause. Multiply by the length of one frame instead.

questions.prompt: At 120 frames per second, how many frames fit in 75 ms?
hints: Find the length of one frame first.
A frame lasts 1000 ÷ 120 ms.
Divide the delay by the length of one frame.
questions.onCorrect: Doubling the frame rate doubles the number of frames in the same time, so 75 ms is 4.5 frames at 60 frames per second and 9 at 120.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A frame lasts 1000 ÷ 120 = 8.33 ms, so 75 ÷ 8.33 = 9 frames.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count at 60 frames per second. Each frame is half as long at 120, so the same delay holds twice as many.
That divides the delay by the frame rate. Divide it by the length of one frame, 8.33 ms, instead.

questions.prompt: A player's skill has risen from 4 to 7 while the level's challenge stayed at 4. The flow channel in this model is challenge within 1 point of skill. By how many points must the challenge rise to reach the channel's lower edge?
hints: Find the lowest challenge that is within 1 point of skill 7.
The lower edge is one point below the skill.
Subtract the current challenge from that edge.
questions.onCorrect: A fixed challenge ends up too easy for the player, so as skill grows, the challenge has to grow with it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The lower edge of the channel is 7 − 1 = 6, and 6 − 4 = 2 points of challenge.

misconceptions.feedback: That reaches a challenge equal to the skill. The channel starts one point lower.
That is the width of the channel, not the distance to it.
That is the challenge at the start, not a rise. Find the edge first.

questions.prompt: In a course built in waves, wave 1 has challenges 2, 4, 6 and 3 on its four levels, and each later wave starts 2 higher with the same shape. What is the challenge on the last level of wave 3?
hints: Each wave starts two higher than the one before.
Find the first challenge of wave 3.
Keep the shape of wave 1 from that start: up by 2, up by 2, then down by 3.
questions.onCorrect: The valley of each wave is higher than the valley of the one before, so the trend rises even though the line keeps falling.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Wave 3 starts at 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 and has challenges 6, 8, 10 and 7, so its last level has challenge 7.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the peak of wave 3. The last level is the relief level after it.
That is the relief level of wave 1. Each wave starts higher.

questions.prompt: A player of skill 8 meets a level of challenge 3. In the flow model, which state is the player in? Answer with one word.
hints: The challenge is far below the skill.
questions.onCorrect: Challenge far below skill puts the player under the channel, where nothing is demanded.

misconceptions.feedback: Anxiety is the opposite case, where the challenge is far above skill.

questions.prompt: What is the name for a game changing its challenge in response to measured player performance? Give the name or its initials.
hints: The word dynamic is in it, and so is the word adjustment.
questions.onCorrect: The game measures something, such as deaths per level, and moves the challenge in response.

questions.prompt: Trailing cars in a racing game are made faster so the race stays close. What is the main risk of this adaptive approach?
hints: Think about what a player who notices the change would conclude.
questions.onCorrect: Players can sense rubber-banding, and when they do, a win or a loss no longer feels earned.

acceptedIdeas: Players may notice it and feel the result is unfair
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Players may notice it and feel the result is unfair

choices.label: The difficulty curve becomes a straight ramp
Players can no longer choose a difficulty level
Players may notice it and feel the result is unfair
The game becomes too easy to measure

misconceptions.feedback: Measuring is not the issue. The game still measures the race, and the trouble lies in how players read the result.
Selectable difficulty is a separate approach, and adaptive difficulty does not remove it by itself.
The curve can still rise in waves. The risk comes from players seeing the adjustment.

questions.prompt: An enemy starts with 200 health. Each time the player dies three times in a row, the game cuts the enemy's health by 10 percent of its current value. What is the enemy's health after two such adjustments?
hints: Each cut is 10 percent of the current value, so the cut gets smaller.
After one adjustment the enemy has 90 percent of its health.
Take 90 percent of the new value for the second adjustment.
questions.onCorrect: Because every cut applies to the current health, two cuts of 10 percent remove 38 points, not 40.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first adjustment gives 200 × 0.9 = 180, and the second gives 180 × 0.9 = 162.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes 10 percent of the original 200 twice. The second cut applies to the reduced health.
That is the health after one adjustment. The question asks about two.

questions.prompt: A player of low skill faces a level of very high challenge. In the flow model, which state is the player in?
hints: The challenge is far above the skill.
questions.onCorrect: Challenge far above skill puts the player over the channel, where demands outrun ability.

misconceptions.feedback: Boredom is the opposite case, where the challenge is far below the player's skill. Here the challenge is far above it.
Flow needs the challenge to lie within the channel around the player's skill, and a very high challenge against low skill is far outside it.

questions.prompt: Using the same wave pattern, wave 1 starts at challenge 2 and each later wave starts 2 higher. What is the starting challenge of wave 5?
hints: Count how many waves come after wave 1.
Each of those adds 2 to the start.
Add 4 steps of 2 to the first start.
questions.onCorrect: A rising trend with valleys gives the player a steady rise in challenge without a long unbroken climb.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Wave 5 is four steps after wave 1, so it starts at 2 + 4 × 2 = 10.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the start of wave 4. Wave 5 is one step later.
That counts five steps of 2. Wave 1 is the starting point, so there are four steps.

questions.prompt: An enemy starts with 300 health. Each adjustment cuts its health by 20 percent of its current value. What is its health after two adjustments?
hints: After one cut the enemy has 80 percent of its health.
The second cut applies to the reduced health.
Multiply by 0.8 twice.
questions.onCorrect: Two cuts of 20 percent remove 108 points, which is 36 percent of the starting health and not 40.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes 20 percent of the original 300 twice. The second cut applies to the reduced health.
That is the health after one adjustment. The question asks about two.

questions.prompt: A sword hits for 50 damage, and one hit in ten is a critical hit that does triple damage. Roughly how much damage does a hit do on average?
hints: Most hits are ordinary hits.
A critical hit does 100 more than an ordinary hit, but it happens only one time in ten.
questions.onCorrect: Only one hit in ten is critical, so the average is pulled a little above the ordinary 50 and no further.

misconceptions.feedback: 150 is the damage of a critical hit alone, and only one hit in ten is critical. The other nine do 50.
100 would be about right only if ordinary and critical hits were equally common. Nine hits in ten are ordinary, so the average stays much nearer 50.
One hit in ten does 150, which is 100 more than an ordinary hit, so the average must lie above 50 even though no single hit does more than that on most swings.

questions.prompt: A sword hits for 50 damage. It misses 30 percent of the time, and 10 percent of its hits are critical hits that do 150. What is the expected damage per swing?
hints: Find the probability of each of the three outcomes.
A critical hit needs a hit first, so multiply 0.7 by 0.1.
Add each probability times its damage.
questions.onCorrect: A miss chance multiplies the whole expected value by the chance of hitting, so 60 × 0.7 gives the same result.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A miss does 0, a plain hit has probability 0.7 × 0.9 = 0.63 and does 50, and a critical hit has probability 0.7 × 0.1 = 0.07 and does 150, so 0 + 31.5 + 10.5 = 42.

misconceptions.feedback: That ignores the misses. Three swings in ten do nothing.
That is the damage of a plain hit. Weight the plain hit, the crit and the miss by their probabilities.

questions.prompt: Time to kill is the target's health divided by what quantity? Give the name or its initials.
hints: The answer is a rate, in damage for each second.
questions.onCorrect: Dividing health by a damage rate gives seconds directly.

questions.prompt: An enemy has 240 health. A weapon does 40 damage per hit and hits 3 times per second. How many seconds does it take to kill the enemy?
hints: First find the damage per second.
Multiply the damage per hit by the hits per second.
Divide the health by that rate.
questions.onCorrect: Doubling the damage rate halves the time to kill, which is why small changes to speed have large effects.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The weapon deals 40 × 3 = 120 damage per second, and 240 ÷ 120 = 2 seconds.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the health by the damage per hit, giving a count of hits. Divide by damage per second instead.
That divides by 240 where the damage per second should be. First find the damage per second.

questions.prompt: An upgrade costs 80 × 1.5^(level − 1). What does level 3 cost?
hints: The exponent is the level minus 1.
1.5 squared is 2.25.
Multiply 80 by that.
questions.onCorrect: Each level costs half as much again as the one before, so the increases themselves grow.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Level 3 uses the exponent 3 − 1 = 2, so the cost is 80 × 1.5² = 80 × 2.25 = 180.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the cost of level 2, whose exponent is 1.
That multiplies by 3 for level 3. The growth is a power of 1.5, not a multiple of the level.
That multiplies 80 by 1.5 and by 3. The exponent is the level minus 1.

questions.prompt: Players earn 500 coins per hour and the shops absorb 350 coins per hour. After 4 hours of play, how many more coins are held by players than at the start?
hints: Find the coins gained and the coins removed each hour.
The difference is the surplus per hour.
Multiply the surplus by the hours.
questions.onCorrect: A steady surplus keeps growing, which is why designers look for sinks that grow with the sources.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The surplus is 500 − 350 = 150 coins per hour, and over 4 hours it is 4 × 150 = 600.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the surplus after one hour. The question covers four hours.
That is the coins earned in four hours. Some of them were spent.

questions.prompt: Using cost = 100 × 1.5^(level − 1), at which level does the cost first exceed 500?
hints: Work out the cost for each level in turn.
Each cost is 1.5 times the one before.
Look for the first cost above 500.
questions.onCorrect: Costs that grow by a fixed ratio pass any limit surprisingly soon, which is how an exponential curve can stall a player.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Costs for levels 1 to 6 are 100, 150, 225, 337.5, 506.25 and 759.4, and level 5 is the first above 500.

misconceptions.feedback: Level 6 does exceed it, but an earlier level already does.
Level 4 costs 337.5, which is still below 500.

questions.prompt: A hit does 40 damage. One hit in four is a critical hit that does double damage. What is the expected damage per hit?
hints: Weight each outcome by its probability.
Double damage is 80, with probability 0.25.
questions.onCorrect: Expected damage rises with both the crit chance and the multiplier, so the two are traded against each other.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three hits in four do 40 and one in four does 80, so 0.75 × 40 + 0.25 × 80 = 30 + 20 = 50.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the damage of a critical hit alone. Most hits are not critical.
That averages 40 and 80 as if each were equally likely. The crit happens one time in four.

questions.prompt: An enemy has 500 health. A weapon does 80 damage per hit and hits 2.5 times per second. How many seconds does it take to kill the enemy?
hints: First find the damage per second.
Multiply 80 by 2.5.
Divide the health by the damage per second.
questions.onCorrect: The time to kill is the design number players feel, because it sets how long a fight lasts.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The weapon deals 80 × 2.5 = 200 damage per second, and 500 ÷ 200 = 2.5 seconds.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the health by the damage per hit, which gives a count of hits. Divide by the damage per second instead.
That is the damage per second. The question asks how long it takes to deal 500.

questions.prompt: An upgrade costs 50 × 2^(level − 1). What does level 5 cost?
hints: The exponent is the level minus 1.
2 to the power 4 is 16.
Multiply 50 by that.
questions.onCorrect: A doubling curve makes the fifth upgrade 16 times as expensive as the first.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The exponent is 5 − 1 = 4, so the cost is 50 × 16 = 800.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies 50 by 10, as if the cost rose by 2 per level in a straight line. The power of 2 grows faster.
That uses the exponent 3 where the exponent should be the level minus 1.

questions.prompt: In a paper test each player starts with 12 coins. Every round a player earns 1 coin and then pays 3 for a card. How many coins does a player hold after 4 rounds?
hints: Find the change in coins over one round.
Each round the player earns 1 and pays 3.
Add that change four times to the starting 12.
questions.onCorrect: With a net loss of two coins a round, the 4 coins left last only two more rounds, which a designer can see from a few minutes of dealing.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each round changes the total by 1 − 3 = −2, so after 4 rounds the total is 12 − 8 = 4 coins.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the cost instead of subtracting it. The player pays 3 each round.
That counts the earnings and forgets the cost of the cards.
That assumes the coins have run out already. Work out the change in one round and apply it four times.

questions.prompt: A team wants to learn whether the first room of a prototype is clear. Which question can a playtest answer?
hints: A testable question can be answered by watching what a player does.
questions.onCorrect: The question names something a tester either does or does not do within a limit, so observation can settle it.

acceptedIdeas: Can players find the exit of the first room within 2 minutes?
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Can players find the exit of the first room within 2 minutes?

choices.label: Is the game fun for everyone?
Is the first room well designed?
Can players find the exit of the first room within 2 minutes?

misconceptions.feedback: Liking is an opinion, and players are polite. Watching what they do is stronger evidence.
Well designed has no observable meaning until it is turned into something a player does.
Fun for everyone is far too wide for one session, and no observation settles it.

questions.prompt: 90 players beat level 1 and so reach level 2, and 45 of them beat level 2. What percentage of those who reached level 2 beat it?
hints: Divide the players who beat level 2 by the players who reached it.
The players who reached level 2 are the ones who beat level 1.
Turn the fraction into a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Measuring each step against the players who reached it makes the steps comparable.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 45 of the 90 who reached level 2 beat it, and 45 ÷ 90 = 0.5, which is 50 percent.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 200, which counts everyone who started. Only those who reached level 2 had a chance to beat it.
That is the number who beat level 2, not a percentage of those who reached it.

questions.prompt: Share kept at a step = players who got through it ÷ players who ___ the step. Which verb fits? Answer with one word.
hints: Which players had the chance to get through the step?
questions.onCorrect: Only players who reached a step could have got through it, so they are the right denominator.

questions.prompt: 300 players started, 240 finished the tutorial and 180 beat level 1. What percentage of those who finished the tutorial beat level 1?
hints: Divide by the players who finished the tutorial.
Do not divide by the 300 who started.
Turn the fraction into a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: A step's share tells you how many reached it and stayed, which is the figure to track across versions.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 180 of the 240 who finished the tutorial beat level 1, and 180 ÷ 240 = 0.75, which is 75 percent.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by the 300 who started. Level 1 could only be attempted by those who finished the tutorial.
That is the count who beat level 1, not a percentage.

questions.prompt: After easing level 2, a new group of 200 players gives this funnel: 150 finished the tutorial, 100 beat level 1 and 65 beat level 2. What percentage of those who reached level 2 beat it?
hints: Find who reached level 2.
Those who beat level 1 reached level 2.
Divide the players who beat level 2 by that number.
questions.onCorrect: Level 2 went from keeping half of its players to keeping most of them, from a change to one thing, while the other steps stayed within a few points.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 players reached level 2 and 65 of them beat it, so the share is 65 ÷ 100 = 65 percent.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 200, which counts everyone who started. Divide by the players who reached level 2.
That divides by the 150 who finished the tutorial. The players who reached level 2 are those who beat level 1.

questions.prompt: 400 players started, 300 finished the tutorial and 120 beat level 1. What percentage of those who finished the tutorial beat level 1?
hints: Divide by the players who finished the tutorial.
The 400 who started are not the right base.
Turn the fraction into a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Shares of those who reached each step show where a design loses players, and the counts alone do not.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 120 of the 300 who finished the tutorial beat level 1, and 120 ÷ 300 = 0.4, which is 40 percent.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by the 400 who started. Divide by those who finished the tutorial.
That is the count, not a percentage.

questions.prompt: In a paper test each player starts with 20 coins, earns 1 coin a round and pays 4 coins for a card each round. After how many whole rounds can a player no longer afford the next card, if coins must stay at zero or above?
hints: Find the net change of one round.
Each round loses 4 − 1 coins.
Divide the starting coins by that loss and keep the whole rounds.
questions.onCorrect: A short paper test shows that this economy drains a player in about seven rounds, which can be fixed before anything is built.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each round loses 3 coins, so after 6 rounds the player holds 20 − 18 = 2 coins, and the 7th payment would leave −1, so 6 rounds can be completed.

misconceptions.feedback: In the 7th round the player would end with a negative number of coins, so only the rounds before it are completed.
After 5 rounds the player still has coins to spare. Keep counting while the total stays at zero or above.

questions.prompt: What do designers call the in-game events that a game logs to show where players fail or quit?
hints: The word begins with tele, as in measuring from a distance.
questions.onCorrect: Telemetry records what players did without anyone having to watch them.

questions.prompt: A loop moves a ball 5 pixels on each pass and runs 120 times per second. How many pixels does the ball move in one second?
hints: Count the passes in one second.
Each pass moves the ball by 5 pixels.
Multiply the passes by the pixels per pass.
questions.onCorrect: At 60 passes per second the same code gives 300 pixels, so the ball is twice as fast on the faster machine.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The ball moves 5 pixels per pass and makes 120 passes, so 5 × 120 = 600 pixels in one second.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the distance on a machine that runs the loop 60 times per second.
That adds the numbers where the passes should be multiplied by the distance per pass.

questions.prompt: A ball moves at 900 pixels per second and the game updates 30 times per second. How many pixels does it move on each update?
hints: The distance per update is the speed divided by the updates per second.
Divide 900 by the number of updates in a second.
Compare the answer with a wall that is 10 pixels thick.
questions.onCorrect: A step longer than a thin object means the ball may never be recorded inside it, a failure called tunnelling.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each update covers 900 ÷ 30 = 30 pixels, three times the 10-pixel thickness of the wall, so the ball can jump over it.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the speed by the update rate. A larger update rate makes each step shorter, so divide.
That is the distance per update at 60 updates per second.

questions.prompt: The step is 20 ms. A frame takes 110 ms and the lag starts at 0. How many updates run?
hints: Add the frame time to the lag.
Count how many whole steps of 20 ms fit in the lag.
110 ÷ 20 gives a whole part and a remainder.
questions.onCorrect: The remainder is not lost: it stays in the accumulator and counts towards the next frame.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The lag is 110 ms, and each update spends 20 ms, so 5 updates run (100 ms) and 10 ms remain.

misconceptions.feedback: That rounds 110 ÷ 20 up. An update runs only when a whole step of 20 ms is available.
Updates come in whole steps. Count the whole steps in the lag.

questions.prompt: What is the leftover real time carried from one frame to the next called? Give the name that is used for the variable that holds it.
hints: It collects unspent time, like a running total.
questions.onCorrect: Each update spends one step from it, and whatever remains waits for the next frame.

questions.prompt: The step is 20 ms and the lag starts at 0. Frames take 70, 25, 5 and 40 ms in turn. How many updates run in total over the four frames?
hints: Run the accumulator one frame at a time, carrying the remainder.
After the second frame the remainder is 15 ms.
Add the 5 ms frame to that remainder, then spend whole steps.
questions.onCorrect: Over the four frames the loop received 140 ms of real time, and 7 steps of 20 ms use exactly that much.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The updates per frame are 3 (lag 70, leaving 10), 1 (35, leaving 15), 1 (20, leaving 0) and 2 (40, leaving 0), which add up to 7.

misconceptions.feedback: That skips the update in the third frame. The 15 ms left over plus the 5 ms that arrives makes a whole step.
That counts the frames in which at least one update ran. A frame can run several.

questions.prompt: The previous update put an object at x = 100 and the latest at x = 120. The step is 20 ms and the lag is 5 ms. At what x is the object drawn?
hints: Divide the lag by the step to get a fraction.
The fraction is between 0 and 1.
Go that fraction of the way from 100 to 120.
questions.onCorrect: Drawing between the two updates lets the picture move smoothly even when the update rate and the frame rate do not match.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The fraction is 5 ÷ 20 = 0.25, so the drawn position is 100 + 0.25 × (120 − 100) = 105.

misconceptions.feedback: That draws the latest update. A frame is drawn part of the way between the last two.
That uses a fraction of one half, from 10 ms of lag. Divide the actual lag by the step.

questions.prompt: The step is 20 ms and a frame stalls for 500 ms. The loop caps the frame time at 250 ms before adding it to the lag, which starts at 0. How many updates run?
hints: Apply the cap before adding the frame to the lag.
The lag cannot exceed 250 ms.
Count the whole steps of 20 ms in 250 ms.
questions.onCorrect: Without the cap the loop would try to run 25 updates, and if each took long enough the lag would never shrink.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The frame time is capped at 250 ms, and 250 ÷ 20 = 12.5, so 12 updates run and 10 ms remain.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the whole 500 ms, which the cap does not allow.
That rounds 250 ÷ 20 up. Updates run only for whole steps.

questions.prompt: The step is 20 ms. A frame takes 90 ms and the lag starts at 0. How many updates run?
hints: Add the frame time to the lag.
Count the whole steps of 20 ms in the lag.
90 ÷ 20 gives a whole part and a remainder.
questions.onCorrect: Four updates for a 90 ms frame show why a slow frame is followed by a burst of updates.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The lag is 90 ms, so 4 whole steps of 20 ms run (80 ms).

misconceptions.feedback: That rounds 90 ÷ 20 up. An update runs only when a whole step is available.
Updates come in whole steps.

questions.prompt: Same setup: the step is 20 ms and one frame of 90 ms arrives with no lag waiting. How many milliseconds of lag remain after the updates?
hints: Find how many whole steps ran.
Multiply the updates by the step.
Subtract the time spent from the lag.
questions.onCorrect: That 10 ms is carried into the next frame and is not lost.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four updates spend 80 ms of the 90 ms, leaving 10 ms.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time the updates spent. The question asks for what is left.
The lag is not a whole number of steps, so some remains.

questions.prompt: A game moves objects by speed × delta time on every frame. What problem can remain?
hints: Think about what happens when a frame takes much longer than usual.
questions.onCorrect: Scaling by delta time keeps average speed but not the path taken, which depends on the size of each step.

acceptedIdeas: Results can still differ between machines, and fast objects can pass through thin walls
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Results can still differ between machines, and fast objects can pass through thin walls

choices.label: The objects move more slowly on faster machines
Objects stop moving whenever the frame time changes
Results can still differ between machines, and fast objects can pass through thin walls
The game cannot render at more than 60 frames per second

misconceptions.feedback: Scaling by delta time keeps the distance per second the same, so the speed does not fall on faster machines.
Scaling movement by delta time has no bearing on the render rate.
Objects keep moving. The step they move by changes with the frame time.

questions.prompt: A character has three boolean flags: `isJumping`, `isDucking` and `isDiving`. How many different combinations of values can the three flags hold?
hints: List the values of one flag, then add a second flag.
Each new flag doubles the number of combinations.
Multiply 2 by itself once for each flag.
questions.onCorrect: Only four of the eight combinations correspond to something a character can really be doing.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each flag has 2 values, so three flags give 2 × 2 × 2 = 2³ = 8 combinations.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 2 + 2 + 2. Each flag doubles the combinations so far, which multiplies them.
That is the number of flags, not the number of combinations they can hold.
That is 3 × 3. Each flag has 2 values, not 3.

questions.prompt: A character has the flags `isJumping`, `isDucking` and `isDiving`, and a fourth flag, `isFiring`, is added. How many different combinations of values can the four flags hold?
hints: Each flag doubles the number of combinations.
Start from the number for three flags.
Double it once for the new flag.
questions.onCorrect: The count doubles with every flag, while the number of real states grows only by a few.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four flags give 2⁴ = 16 combinations, double the eight that three flags give.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 4 to 8, as if each flag added a fixed number. Each flag doubles the total.
That is the number of flags, not the combinations they can hold.
That is the count for three flags. The new flag doubles it.

questions.prompt: A transition table has one row for each state and one column for each event. How many cells does a table for 5 states and 3 events have?
hints: A table has a cell for every row and column pair.
Multiply the rows by the columns.
Rows are states and columns are events.
questions.onCorrect: Most cells are usually empty, because most events do nothing in most states.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are 5 rows and 3 columns, so the table has 5 × 3 = 15 cells.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the states and the events. Every state meets every event, so multiply.
That counts the rows only. Each row has a cell for every event.

questions.prompt: In a transition table, what happens to an event for which the current state has no entry? Answer with one word.
hints: The state stays as it was.
questions.onCorrect: A missing entry means that event does nothing in that state, so the machine stays where it is.

questions.prompt: The character starts as standing and receives the events jump, duck, release, land. Release has no entry for the diving state. Which state is it in at the end?
hints: Follow each event from the current state, using the table.
questions.onCorrect: Release does nothing while diving, and land then returns the character to standing.

misconceptions.feedback: Land has an entry for diving, which moves the character out of it. Follow all four events.
Release would end a duck from the ducking state, but the character was diving by then.

questions.prompt: A state object has a method that runs once when the machine moves into it, another that runs every update, and another that runs when it leaves. What is the name of the first one?
hints: The other two are update and exit.
questions.onCorrect: Setup such as choosing a sprite belongs in enter, and cleanup in exit, so neither is repeated every frame.

questions.prompt: Four ground states, standing, walking, running and ducking, each respond to two events, jump and attack, in the same way. A flat machine gives each state its own arrow for each event. How many arrows does a parent state called on the ground save?
hints: Count the arrows without a parent: states times events.
With a parent, each event needs one arrow.
Subtract the second count from the first.
questions.onCorrect: The parent's arrows are inherited by every substate, and a fifth ground state would add no new arrow.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A flat machine needs 4 × 2 = 8 arrows, and a parent state needs only 2, so it saves 8 − 2 = 6.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of arrows in the flat machine. The question asks how many the parent saves.
That is the number of arrows left with a parent, not the number saved.

questions.prompt: A character has five boolean flags. How many combinations of values can they hold?
hints: Each flag doubles the combinations.
Start from 2 for one flag.
Double it four more times.
questions.onCorrect: Only a handful of the 32 combinations would be real states, which is why a single state variable is safer.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Five flags give 2⁵ = 32 combinations.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 5 × 2. Each flag doubles the total, which means repeated multiplication.
That is 5 × 5, but each flag has 2 values.

questions.prompt: A transition table covers 6 states and 4 events. How many cells does it have?
hints: Rows are states and columns are events.
Every state meets every event.
Multiply the rows by the columns.
questions.onCorrect: Each of the 24 cells either names a next state or leaves the state alone.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A cell exists for every state and event pair, so there are 6 × 4 = 24 cells.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the states and events. Multiply them.
That counts the rows only.

questions.prompt: The machine starts in idle. On jump while idle it goes to jumping, and on land while jumping it goes to idle. After the events jump, land, jump, which state is it in?
hints: Follow the three events one at a time.
questions.onCorrect: The second jump moves the machine from idle back to jumping, so it ends where the first jump took it.

misconceptions.feedback: The third event is a jump, which takes the machine out of idle.

questions.prompt: Which design lets a player rebind jump from Space to J without changing any game logic?
hints: Which design puts the key in data and not in code?
questions.onCorrect: The table holds the key, the command does the work, and only the table changes when a key is rebound.

acceptedIdeas: A binding table that maps inputs to commands
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A binding table that maps inputs to commands

choices.label: A binding table that maps inputs to commands

misconceptions.feedback: Each new key adds another branch to the chain, so the game logic is changed whenever a key changes.
A flag records a fact about the game and does not say which key does what.
A singleton is a way of having one instance of a class and says nothing about how inputs reach actions.

questions.prompt: A 60-second match runs at 60 frames per second, so it has 3600 frames. The player made 40 inputs. How many times more records does a recording of every frame need than a recording of one command per input?
hints: Find the number of records for each method.
Frame recording needs one record per frame, command recording one per input.
Divide the larger count by the smaller one.
questions.onCorrect: A replay of commands is also small enough to share, but it works only if the game replays them deterministically.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Every frame needs 3600 records and commands need 40, so 3600 ÷ 40 = 90 times as many.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of command records. The question asks how many times larger the frame recording is.
That adds the two counts. Divide the larger count by the smaller to find how many times as large it is.

questions.prompt: A game stores the commands a player executes so that they can be undone. Commands A, B, C and D are executed in that order, and the player then undoes twice. Which commands are still applied?
hints: Each undo reverses one command.
Which command does an undo reverse first, the oldest or the most recent?
questions.onCorrect: C and D are not deleted yet: they sit in a redo list until a new command is executed.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the result of undoing once. Two undos reverse two commands, so one more has gone than this.
Undo reverses the most recent command first, so D goes first and then C. The oldest commands are the ones that stay applied.
That is the state before any undo. Each undo reverses one command, so after two undos two commands are no longer applied.

questions.prompt: Commands A, B, C and D are executed, the player undoes three times, and then executes a new command E. How many commands are on the undo stack?
hints: Find what the stack holds after the undos.
Executing a new command adds it to the end.
B, C and D are discarded when E is executed.
questions.onCorrect: B, C and D can no longer be redone, because redoing them would now apply them after E in a history that never contained them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: After the undos the stack holds only A, and executing E adds E, so the stack is A, E, which is 2 commands.

misconceptions.feedback: That keeps B, C and D. A new command discards the redo history.
That leaves out E itself. Executing a new command pushes it onto the stack after A.

questions.prompt: When a new command is executed after some undos, what happens to the undone commands waiting to be redone? Answer with one word.
hints: They cannot be redone any longer.
questions.onCorrect: The redo branch is cleared, because it describes a future that no longer follows from the new history.

questions.prompt: Commands A, B, C, D, E and F are executed. The player undoes 3 times, executes G, then undoes once. How many commands are applied now?
hints: Work out which commands are applied after the three undos.
G is added after them and discards the undone commands.
The final undo reverses G.
questions.onCorrect: G is now the only command that can be redone, since D, E and F were discarded when G was executed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Undoing 3 of the 6 leaves A, B and C. Executing G makes A, B, C, G, and undoing once leaves A, B and C applied.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves G applied. The final undo reverses it.
That subtracts a further command. The final undo reverses only G.
That ignores the undos.

questions.prompt: A move command stores the old x and y of the object it moved, as two 4-byte numbers. How many bytes does an undo history of 100 such commands need?
hints: Find the bytes one command stores.
Two numbers of 4 bytes each.
Multiply by the number of commands.
questions.onCorrect: A snapshot of the whole game after every move would store the entire world 100 times, which is why commands store only what they need to reverse.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each command stores 2 × 4 = 8 bytes, so 100 commands need 800 bytes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the size of one command. The history holds 100.
That counts 4 bytes per command. Each stores two numbers of 4 bytes.

questions.prompt: Commands A, B, C, D and E are executed. The player undoes twice and then executes F. How many commands are on the undo stack?
hints: Find what the stack holds after the undos.
Two undos remove D and E.
Executing F adds one command.
questions.onCorrect: D and E are discarded when F is executed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: After the undos the stack holds A, B and C, and executing F makes A, B, C, F, which is 4 commands.

misconceptions.feedback: That keeps D and E and adds F. A new command discards the undone ones.
That ignores the undos.

questions.prompt: In the same situation, A to E executed, two undos, then F executed, how many commands can now be redone?
hints: What happens to the redo history when a new command is executed?
The undone commands are discarded.
Count what is left in the redo list.
questions.onCorrect: Redo becomes available again only after the next undo.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Executing F discarded D and E, so nothing remains to be redone.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts D and E, which were discarded when F was executed.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the pattern that wraps a request as an object, so that it can be stored, queued, replayed or undone?
hints: It is the same word as an order given to an actor.
questions.onCorrect: Because an action is an object, it can be put in a table, a queue, a recording or a history.

questions.prompt: A monster can have any of three independent traits: flies, swims, poisons. If every combination of traits needs its own class, how many monster classes are there, counting the monster with no trait?
hints: Each trait is either there or not.
Each new trait doubles the number of combinations.
Multiply 2 by itself once for each trait.
questions.onCorrect: With components the same monsters need three small components and a list, and adding a fourth trait adds one component.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each trait is either present or absent, so the combinations number 2 × 2 × 2 = 2³ = 8.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the traits, not the classes. Each combination of traits needs its own class.
That adds 2 + 2 + 2. The combinations multiply.
That leaves out the monster with no traits, which also needs a class.

questions.prompt: A monster can have any of four independent traits: flies, swims, poisons, breathes fire. If every combination of traits needs its own class, how many monster classes are there, counting the monster with no trait?
hints: Each trait doubles the number of combinations.
Start from the count for three traits.
Double it once for the new trait.
questions.onCorrect: The classes double with every trait while the components grow by one, which is the case for composition.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four traits give 2⁴ = 16 combinations, while components need only four.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of components needed. Inheritance needs a class per combination.
That adds 4 to 8. The new trait doubles the number of combinations.

questions.prompt: In an entity component system, what is the name for a function that loops over every entity having the components it needs, such as moving everything with position and velocity?
hints: Entities are ids and components are data, which leaves one more part.
questions.onCorrect: A system holds the behaviour, so components stay plain data and entities stay bare ids.

questions.prompt: A record holds an entity's position and velocity together, 6 floats of 4 bytes each. How many whole records fit in one 64-byte cache line?
hints: Find the size of one position in bytes.
Six floats of 4 bytes each.
Divide 64 by that size and keep only the whole part.
questions.onCorrect: The remaining 16 bytes hold the start of the next record, or nothing, depending on the layout.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A record is 6 × 4 = 24 bytes, and 64 ÷ 24 = 2.67, so 2 whole records fit, using 48 bytes.

misconceptions.feedback: That rounds 2.67 up. A record that does not fit completely is not a whole record.
That divides 64 by 4, the size of one float. A record is six floats.
That divides 64 by 6. Each float is 4 bytes, so the record is larger than 6 bytes.

questions.prompt: What is the name for the fixed-size block of memory, commonly 64 bytes, that a processor fetches at a time?
hints: It is named for the cache it is fetched into.
questions.onCorrect: The processor fetches a whole line even if the program wants only a few bytes of it.

questions.prompt: A velocity is 2 floats of 4 bytes each, and 800 velocities are stored in one packed array. How many 64-byte cache lines does the array occupy?
hints: Find the bytes in all the velocities.
One velocity is 8 bytes.
Divide the total bytes by 64.
questions.onCorrect: A packed array uses almost every byte of every line it touches.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 800 velocities of 8 bytes make 6400 bytes, and 6400 ÷ 64 = 100 lines.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of velocities. Each takes 8 bytes, and a line holds 64.
That is the size in bytes. Divide it by the 64 bytes in a line.

questions.prompt: An entity record is 64 bytes: position 12, velocity 12, health 4 and 36 of other data. A collision system, which applies damage on impact, needs position, velocity and health. With 2000 entities, how many 64-byte lines does it read from separate arrays of positions, velocities and health values, packed tightly?
hints: Count the bytes the system actually needs for one entity.
Multiply by the 2000 entities.
Divide the total by 64.
questions.onCorrect: An array of whole 64-byte records would touch 2000 lines, since each record fills a line, so the separate arrays touch a little under half as many.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Position, velocity and health take 12 + 12 + 4 = 28 bytes per entity, so 2000 × 28 = 56 000 bytes, and 56 000 ÷ 64 = 875 lines.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of lines when each 64-byte record is read whole. The question concerns separate arrays.
That is the size in bytes. Divide it by 64 to count lines.
That counts only position and velocity. This system also reads the 4 bytes of health for each entity.

questions.prompt: A velocity is 2 floats of 4 bytes each. How many whole velocities fit in one 64-byte cache line?
hints: Find the size of one velocity in bytes.
Two floats of 4 bytes each.
Divide 64 by that size.
questions.onCorrect: Smaller components pack more of them into each line, so more of them arrive for each fetch.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A velocity is 2 × 4 = 8 bytes, and 64 ÷ 8 = 8 velocities.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides 64 by 4. A velocity holds two floats.
That divides 64 by 16, as if a velocity were 16 bytes. Two floats of 4 bytes each are smaller than that.

questions.prompt: A monster can have five independent traits. How many classes does inheritance need if each combination has its own?
hints: Each trait is present or absent.
Each trait doubles the number of combinations.
Multiply 2 by itself five times.
questions.onCorrect: Five components describe all 32 combinations, which is why composition scales better.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Five traits give 2⁵ = 32 combinations, while components need five.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 5 × 5. Each trait has two possibilities, so the combinations multiply by 2 each time.
That is 5 × 2. The combinations multiply by 2 for each trait.

questions.prompt: Which statement about an entity component system is correct?
hints: Think about where the data and the behaviour live.
questions.onCorrect: Behaviour sits in systems and data in components, which lets a system run through many entities of the same shape together.

acceptedIdeas: Entities are ids, components are plain data, and systems loop over entities that have the components they need
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Entities are ids, components are plain data, and systems loop over entities that have the components they need

choices.label: Entities are ids, components are plain data, and systems loop over entities that have the components they need
Every entity is a subclass of a general entity class
It always makes a game faster, whatever the number of entities
Components hold the code that runs every frame, and systems hold the data

misconceptions.feedback: Locality helps when many entities share the same components, and the pattern costs complexity elsewhere, so it is not always faster.
That reverses the roles. Components are data and systems are the code.
Subclassing is the inheritance design that components replace.

questions.prompt: A listener takes 50 ms every time it is called, and the game runs at 60 frames per second, so a frame lasts 16.7 ms. About how many frames' worth of time does one call take?
hints: Use the length of one frame given in the question.
Divide the time the listener takes by the length of a frame.
50 ÷ 16.7 is very close to a whole number.
questions.onCorrect: If the subject waits for the listener, the player sees that much of a stall each time the event fires.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A frame lasts 1000 ÷ 60 = 16.7 ms, and 50 ÷ 16.7 is about 3 frames.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time the listener takes in milliseconds. The question asks how many frames that spans.
That divides the frame length by the listener's time. Divide the listener's time by the frame length.
A single frame lasts 16.7 ms, which is much shorter than the call.

questions.prompt: Four destroyed enemies were never unregistered as listeners of a 'player moved' event, which fires 60 times per second. How many calls per second go to dead listeners?
hints: Every registered listener is called on every event.
Count the dead listeners and the events per second.
Multiply them.
questions.onCorrect: Each such call can crash or act on an object that no longer exists, which is why listeners must be removed when they are destroyed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the 4 dead listeners is called on every event, so 4 × 60 = 240 calls per second.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of dead listeners, called once for each event.
That adds the numbers. Every event calls every dead listener, so multiply.

questions.prompt: A listener takes 50 ms and the subject runs every frame. Which design fits better?
hints: Which design lets the subject carry on without waiting?
questions.onCorrect: A queue lets the subject hand the event over and carry on, and the slow work happens elsewhere or later.

acceptedIdeas: An event queue handled outside the hot path
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An event queue handled outside the hot path

choices.label: An event queue handled outside the hot path

misconceptions.feedback: A synchronous observer would make the subject wait for the whole 50 ms on every call.
A global variable can pass data around but does not decide when listeners run.
Inheritance describes what kind of thing an object is and does not decouple a sender from receivers.

questions.prompt: A ring buffer has capacity 4 and its tail index is 2. Each enqueue writes at the tail and then sets tail = (tail + 1) mod capacity. After three enqueues, what is the tail index?
hints: Apply the rule once for each enqueue.
4 mod 4 is 0, since the index wraps back to the start.
Apply the rule again to the result of each step.
questions.onCorrect: The index never reaches the capacity, so it always names a real slot.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first enqueue gives (2 + 1) mod 4 = 3, the second gives (3 + 1) mod 4 = 0, and the third gives (0 + 1) mod 4 = 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the starting tail. Three enqueues move it on.
That counts on past the end. The index wraps to 0 after 3.
That applies the rule once. Each of the three enqueues moves the tail on by one slot, wrapping after 3.

questions.prompt: Which operation makes a ring buffer's index wrap back to 0 after the last slot? Give its name or its usual abbreviation.
hints: It gives the remainder after division by the capacity.
questions.onCorrect: The remainder after dividing by the capacity is always between 0 and the capacity minus 1.

questions.prompt: A ring buffer has capacity 6 and its tail index is 4. After 5 enqueues, with tail = (tail + 1) mod 6 each time, what is the tail index?
hints: Apply the rule once for each enqueue.
The index wraps to 0 after 5.
Count five steps on from 4, wrapping at 6.
questions.onCorrect: Adding all the steps at once and taking the remainder gives the same result.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The tail goes 5, 0, 1, 2, 3 over the five enqueues, so it ends at 3, which is (4 + 5) mod 6.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds without wrapping. The index must stay below the capacity.
That is the starting tail, before any enqueue.

questions.prompt: A player-died event has three synchronous listeners that take 3 ms, 8 ms and 40 ms. How many milliseconds does the damage code wait before it can carry on?
hints: Synchronous listeners run one after another.
The subject waits for the last of them.
Add the three times.
questions.onCorrect: That wait is more than three frames at 60 frames per second, and it grows with every listener added.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The listeners run one after another and the damage code waits for all of them, so the wait is 3 + 8 + 40 = 51 ms.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the slowest listener only. The listeners run one after another, so the times add.
That leaves out the slowest listener, which the subject also waits for.

questions.prompt: A ring buffer has capacity 6 and its tail index is 0. After 8 enqueues, with tail = (tail + 1) mod 6 each time, what is the tail index?
hints: Apply the rule once for each enqueue.
The index returns to 0 after 6 enqueues.
Two more enqueues follow.
questions.onCorrect: Six enqueues bring the tail all the way round, so only the remainder of the count matters.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Eight steps from 0 give 8 mod 6 = 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That does not wrap. The index must stay below the capacity.
That equals the capacity, which wraps back to 0.

questions.prompt: A ring buffer has capacity 4 and its tail index is 1. After 7 enqueues, with tail = (tail + 1) mod 4 each time, what is the tail index?
hints: Apply the rule once for each enqueue.
The index returns to where it started after 4 enqueues.
Count the remaining enqueues from there.
questions.onCorrect: The tail has gone round the ring almost twice and landed on slot 0.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Seven steps from 1 give (1 + 7) mod 4 = 8 mod 4 = 0.

misconceptions.feedback: That does not wrap. The index must stay below the capacity.
That counts only three steps from the start. Add up all seven enqueues.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the pattern in which a subject keeps a list of listeners and notifies each of them when something happens, without knowing what they do?
hints: The listeners watch the subject.
questions.onCorrect: The subject only knows that listeners exist, which keeps systems such as audio and achievements out of the damage code.

questions.prompt: A game keeps three bullet slots. Four bullets are fired in a row and none has expired. How many of the four are refused because no slot is free?
hints: Count the slots that are available.
Each bullet takes one slot.
Subtract the slots from the shots fired.
questions.onCorrect: A fixed number of slots means a decision is needed for the fourth shot: refuse it, overwrite the oldest, or grow the pool.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three bullets take the three slots, so the fourth finds none free, and 4 − 3 = 1 bullet is refused.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of bullets that found a slot. The question asks how many were refused.
That counts every shot. Three of them found a free slot.
A pool has only the slots it reserved, so the fourth shot has nowhere to go.

questions.prompt: A pool has 4 slots. Three bullets are fired, then two of them expire, and then 5 more are fired with none expiring. How many of the last 5 are refused?
hints: Work out how many slots are active after the expiries.
The free slots are the capacity minus the active slots.
Subtract the free slots from the shots fired.
questions.onCorrect: Slots that expire return to the pool at once, so the pool is only ever as full as the number of bullets alive.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: After the first three shots and two expiries, 1 slot is active and 3 are free. Three of the 5 new shots take free slots, and the other 2 are refused.

misconceptions.feedback: That assumes every shot finds a slot. Only the free slots can be used.
That counts only one active slot. Subtract the free slots from the five new shots.
That is the number of free slots when the new shots begin, not the number refused.

questions.prompt: 6,000 trees each have 12 bytes of position, and they share one mesh of 20,000 bytes. What is the total memory in bytes?
hints: The mesh is stored once.
The positions are stored once for each tree.
Add the mesh to the total of the positions.
questions.onCorrect: Without sharing, the same trees need 120,072,000 bytes, about 1,305 times as much.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The mesh is stored once and the positions 6,000 times, so 20,000 + 6,000 × 12 = 20,000 + 72,000 = 92,000 bytes.

misconceptions.feedback: That gives every tree its own copy of the mesh. The trees share one.
That counts only the positions. The shared mesh is stored once and counts too.
That counts only the mesh. Each tree also keeps its own position.

questions.prompt: In the flyweight pattern, what is the name for data that is the same for every instance and never changes, such as a tree's mesh? Answer with one word.
hints: The opposite is extrinsic.
questions.onCorrect: Intrinsic data is safe to share because no instance changes it, so one copy can serve every instance.

misconceptions.feedback: Extrinsic data differs from one instance to the next, such as position, and is stored per instance.

questions.prompt: 2,000 enemies share one 50,000-byte sprite and each keeps 20 bytes of its own state. What is the total memory in bytes?
hints: The sprite is stored once.
The per-enemy state is stored 2,000 times.
Add the two amounts.
questions.onCorrect: Sharing the sprite means the cost of each extra enemy is only its own 20 bytes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sprite is stored once and the state 2,000 times, so 50,000 + 2,000 × 20 = 50,000 + 40,000 = 90,000 bytes.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the per-enemy state. The shared sprite counts once.
That gives each enemy its own copy of the sprite. They share one.

questions.prompt: Which of these belongs in the flyweight, the data shared by all the trees?
hints: Shared data must be identical for every tree and never change.
questions.onCorrect: The mesh is identical for every tree of one kind, so it can be stored once and referenced.
